Burgomaster and Council of Kempten ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to make their Burgomaster available to the Council delegation of Kempten, so that he may accompany them to Nürnberg to the Emperor, where a dispute between the city and the monastery of Kempten is to be settled on 29 June. They ask for a written answer with the messenger.

Bailiff, Ammann and Council of Arbon inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that Fischer of Arbon were expelled from the market when they wanted to offer their fish. They ask the St. Gallen authorities not to allow this anymore, or else, if there are good reasons for it, to inform them of this. They ask for a written answer with the messenger.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen write to Georg Schröttel, Procurator at the imperial court, and ask him to inform them in writing with the same messenger what Doctor Hux, who has demanded 1000 gulden from the Abbot of St. Gallen, has negotiated at the imperial court and what he has told in inns and other places. Furthermore, they inform him that he may keep the money he still has from them, and ask him to inform them whether there are any other news, since the citizens of St. Gallen have given the Emperor a lot of money.

Burgomaster and Council of Wangen inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they are grateful to the citizens of St. Gallen for their advice, after they had had problems with the Emperor regarding the accession to the Schwäbischen Städtebund. Now Count Hugo von Werdenberg had presented their Burgomaster Ulrich Klein, while the latter was staying in Konstanz, with an imperial mandate, of which the citizens of Wangen have enclosed a copy with this letter, in which they were required to appear on 25 October in Reutlingen. The Council delegation of Wangen therefore joins the Council delegation of Ravensburg. They ask the citizens of St. Gallen for further advice and for a written answer with the same messenger.

Burgomaster and Council of Esslingen inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have taken a man named Georg Muruss of Kempten into custody for counterfeiting and that he also confessed to thefts. In an attached note, they inform the citizens of St. Gallen what these thefts were, so that any suspects may be exonerated. They ask the citizens of St. Gallen to inform them in writing, by the same messenger, whether these statements are true.

Hans Studer informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that his horse, which he had lodged with Jakob Zili, was unlawfully sold at the auction, and asks them to ensure that he receives compensation.

Anna von Frischingen, citizen of St. Gallen, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to inform her messenger, who presents this letter, in writing whether they had received an answer concerning the sum of money deposited with the Council of Schwäbisch Gmünd.

Heinrich Reischl, citizen of St. Gallen, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to intervene so that he does not have to repay his debts, which he owes among others to a Schweitzer of Wil, at a later date, although he was convicted by a court at which he could not be present due to absence from the country and the severe illness of his wife. If this should not be possible, he asks them to ensure that the citizens of St. Gallen, to whom he still owes money, are paid first.

The Council messengers at the Diet in Baden ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to send a Council message to Luzern on 8 July, where the following day it is to be discussed how to prevent the Reisläuferei, as it causes great damage.
Burgomaster and Council of Buchhorn ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to provide, at the request of their citizen Zollikofer, one or two persons to support him in a dispute.

Jakob Streif, town physician in Landsberg am Lech, thanks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for their help and offers his help. He says that he has received information about the situation from princes, counts, prelates, lords, and commoners. With his help, damages in the amount of four to five thousand pounds could be avoided every year. If the people of St. Gallen want to know more, they should write to him in Landsberg.

The Council messengers of the Confederates in Luzern inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have learned that the St. Gallen citizens are not enforcing the order decided upon in Luzern, which was intended to prevent mercenary service. They therefore demand that the St. Gallen citizens execute rebels who do not wish to abide by the ban on mercenary service, which the other Confederates will also do.

Schultheiss and Council of Luzern inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the Abbot of Einsiedeln has granted the benefice at Sarmenstorf to Johannes Rissler for his merits, and that Hans Schanner erroneously received the same benefice from the Pope and passed it on to the citizen of St. Gallen Kaspar Wirth. Since the Abbot of Einsiedeln has confirmed that this benefice is free from papal claims, they ask the St. Gallen authorities to speak with Kaspar Wirth so that he waives his claims.

Abbot Ulrich Rösch of the Benedictine monastery of St. Gallen informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he has received news from his embassy, which he had delegated to Zürich because of the discord, and that he now forwards it to them at the request of the former Burgomaster Varnbüler, who is also staying in Zürich.
Burgomaster and Council of Wangen ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to sell them 100 lances. They ask for an answer with the messenger.

Ammann and Council of Bregenz request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, in the name of their citizen Lienhard Ebner, to preserve the inheritance of his deceased brother-in-law Hans Märk, the brother of Lienhard Ebner's wife and of the Barefoot Monk who delivers this letter, until Ebner can attend to it.

Ammann and Council of Appenzell inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that Gallus Kapfmann, Hänsli Oppertshofer and others, citizens of St. Gallen, are withholding from the widow of Hans Oppertshofer her inheritance in the city of St. Gallen. Since the widow and her deceased husband were citizens of Rheineck, the court there is the competent one, which the Appenzellers have already communicated to the St. Gallens through Ammann Zidler, a member of the Council of Appenzell. The Appenzellers ask the St. Gallens to ensure that the seizure of the inheritance is lifted. If the aforementioned citizens of St. Gallen do not want to hand over the inheritance to the widow Oppertshofer, she should have the matter heard before the court in Rheineck. The Appenzellers ask for a written reply with the same messenger.

The Council messengers at the Confederate Diet in Luzern inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they will write to the mercenaries who are staying in Frankreich, telling them that they should return home and that they will then be granted mitigation or exemption from punishment. For with the mercenaries one symbolically loses the rye, of which one then suffers a shortage, and the King treats the mercenaries justly only when he needs them, otherwise they are kept worse than dogs. They urge the St. Gallen authorities to do the same and to send this letter to Luzern within eight days, so that it, together with the letters of the other cantons, can be delivered to the mercenaries.

Hans Billing, citizen of St. Gallen, reports to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he got into a dispute with Ruedi Altherr, Konrad Varnbüler, the young Ramsberg, and Walter Varnbüler when he demanded from Martin Drumschläger, a member of the Gotteshaus, the half gulden that he owed him and had sworn to pay before the court. That these citizens of the city took the side of a member of the Gotteshaus who pays neither taxes nor performs watch duty astonishes him. Altherr and the others had torn up the debt note after the offer of peace and reported him to Burgomaster Vogelweider. When the latter did not want to hear him, Billing insulted him, whereupon he was taken into custody. Billing asks the Burgomaster and Council to release him and declares himself ready to settle any disputes before the court. He asks for a written answer.

Anna von Frischingen writes to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, that she had to leave the city for health reasons and therefore renounces her citizenship of St. Gallen. Furthermore, she asks that her life annuity, which she had acquired, be sent to Augsburg.

Ursula Ruchenacker asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for help in a marriage matter. Her husband has a mistress and holds her captive on the Steinerburg in Steinach. She is treated badly by him and his mistress and must additionally care for their child.

Beda Miles reports to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he allowed himself to be persuaded by a hatter named Sigel to buy Wiler cloth with the money of his Vogtkinder, which Sigel wanted to take to Nördlingen to sell there, which is supposed to bring a large profit, whereby, according to Miles, Felix Täschler and Sebastian Brenk were present as witnesses. However, Sigel did not keep the agreement, whereupon the Under-Burgomaster allowed Miles to send Othmar Flechsner with the cloth to Nördlingen. Miles mentions that this matter means a loss of at least ten gulden for the estate of his Vogtkinder, for which he holds Sigel responsible.

Benedikt von Watt asks the former Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to help him obtain his property, to which he is entitled, for which his brother Konrad has already asked them in a letter. He suffers great distress, and there is a danger that his wife and children would die of hunger.

Benedikt von Watt, who was supported by the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen in a difficult time and received a bond from his brother David, which, however, does not bring in enough to survive, writes to the former Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he has realized that his former way of life was foolish. He asks them to help him to the inheritance of his cousin Hans von Watt.

Johann Rot, Lesemeister in Zürich, writes to his cousin Klaus Rot that he would now, after the Barfüsser Herr Peter had to leave St. Gallen, gladly return there, and asks him to see to it that either this messenger or a town messenger receives a letter from the St. Gallen Council as soon as possible, so that the gentlemen in Konstanz would consent to the transfer and the Bishop, who is currently staying in Zürich, is informed.

Ammann, Court and Kirchhöre of Thal request the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to grant the vacated benefice to Ulrich Girtanner, the Kaplan of Thal, as he has proven himself a pious priest and is from the city of St. Gallen.

The Schultheiss and Council of Winterthur report to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have learned from the priest Konrad Hirt, born in Wil, that the position of assistant priest in St. Gallen is vacant. They issue a letter of recommendation for Konrad Hirt and ask the St. Gallen authorities not to give credence to any potential ill will or slander against the priest.

Ulrich Rösch, Abbot of the Benedictine monastery of St. Gallen, informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he has received the commission from the Emperor to settle the dispute between Rudolf Wirt and his creditors, for which reason he has convened a court day. He has now learned that the citizens of St. Gallen had allowed the creditors to seize and confiscate Wirt's property. The Abbot asks the Council of St. Gallen to instruct the creditors to observe the day appointed by him and thereby not to be disobedient to the Emperor. He sends them a copy of the imperial commission.

Dominikus Frauenfeld, bailiff at Rheineck, informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that their council friends and fellow citizens Gallus Kapfmann and Hans Schwanberg and others had seized the rights to a property that Magdalena Oppertshofer had inherited from her husband Hans and wanted to confiscate it. Since Magdalena is a citizen of Rheineck, he asks the St. Gallen authorities to settle the dispute in Rheineck, or where it seems convenient to them. He asks for a reply with the messenger.

Hans von Hohenlandenberg informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that his cousin Jakob von Schönau might be able to lend money, which they could receive in Winterthur. Otherwise, he could also lend money to the citizens of St. Gallen. Although he is in negotiations regarding an estate, these are not yet far advanced, and he could also withdraw from them. In addition, some persons have asked him for a loan and offered him interest payments (Gülten) in Rapperswil in return, which would be advantageous for him, yet he prefers to make the money available to the city of St. Gallen. He asks for a reply.

Johannes Schenkli, town clerk of St. Gallen, informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he met in Konstanz with the knight Jakob von Schönau, who is willing to lend the citizens of St. Gallen two and a half thousand gulden. He says that he wrote to his cousin Hans von Hohenlandenberg, telling him to meet him in Neuenburg. Schenkli reported to Jakob von Schönau about the negotiations with Hans von Hohenlandenberg and asks the citizens of St. Gallen to send a copy of the agreement to Jakob von Schönau. Schenkli also asks the citizens of St. Gallen to inform him when they intend to send their council messenger to Neuenburg, so that he can draw up the contract. Furthermore, he says that he found Mitgülten for the money, which is to be handed over to the hospital for an interest and a life annuity. He says that he received the one thousand gulden of Frau Mangolt. In addition, he asks that the citizens of St. Gallen collect the interest owed to Frau Schwarzach and send it to him. In the matter of Heinrich Stetter, Schenkli wishes to report in person to the Burgomaster and Council the following day and also to inform Heinrich Göldli about this.

Burgomaster and Council of Ulm inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they must build a new mang. They ask the St. Gallen authorities to show their mangs to their master builder Michael Wirtemberg, who presents this letter, so that he can also build one in Ulm.

Albrecht Miles, Landvogt of the County of Toggenburg, asks Klaus Rot, Deputy Burgomaster of St. Gallen, to use his influence, as discussed in Lichtensteig, for the safety of his brother-in-law Hug von Watt, and that the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen contact him, Albrecht, directly if Hug is accused, so that he can advocate for him and satisfy the citizens of St. Gallen. He asks for a reply.

Heinrich von Hewen, Dekan, and Johannes Zwick, Domherr, both Guardians of the Cathedral in Konstanz, inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the church is owed two gulden in interest from Daniel Spenglers house in the Spisergasse and 12 schillings in interest from Ambrosius Spenglers house in the Kirchhof in St. Gallen, which have not been paid in the last two years. They therefore ask to be informed if the houses are confiscated, so that the Cathedral does not lose these interests.

Konrad Üsslinger zu Villingen and Hans Bletz von Rotenstein ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to pay the interest, namely eighty gulden for Konrad and 20 gulden for Hans, which would have been due on 25 May, in Villingen, as they need the money. They ask for a written answer with the messenger.

Ammann and Council of Glarus request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to grant a benefice in the hospital to the citizen of St. Gallen Rudolf Eckel, who presents this letter, as he can no longer provide for his own sustenance due to his age.

Burgomaster and Council of Überlingen inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that, after the grain purchase had repeatedly been the subject of their correspondence with St. Gallen, they learned on this day that the St. Gallen grain buyers had told the sellers in the Überlingen Gredhaus that they would pay the day's highest price for the entire grain, which does not correspond to the customs, whereby the Überlinger would have most liked to have put the St. Gallen grain buyers in custody, but they refrained from doing so.

Michael Muntprat and Othmar Spengler of Konstanz report to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they had heard that several citizens of St. Gallen, among them Hans Renftler, were speaking ill of them, which harmed their honour. They ask them to set a court day so that the matter can be clarified. They also ask for free escort to this day. Otherwise, Michael Muntprat and Othmar Spengler would have to see for themselves how they could come to their right. They ask for a written answer with the messenger.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have Kaspar Stump of Mühlheim in custody, who is supposed to have murdered a journeyman in the Welschland near Genf, which he however did not confess. On the contrary, he had beaten Mittelhans von der Reichenau at that time and received money from him, of which he returned a part. The men of Zürich located Mittelhans, who however described the incident as more serious. Kaspar Stump claims that Mittelhans described the incident more severely out of spite, and named Jörg Spörly of St. Gallen as a witness to the incident. The men of Zürich ask the men of St. Gallen to inquire with Jörg Spörly what happened, and ask for a written answer with the same messenger.

Ammann and Council of Appenzell confirm to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen the content of a letter concerning the St. Gallen citizen Widenhuber and report that the Widenhubers had presented their dispute with an Appenzeller to them in the presence of two St. Gallen guild masters. The Appenzellers have delegated members of their Council to settle the matter with the help of the St. Gallen. If this should not succeed, the parties to the dispute should state whether they wished to pursue the matter judicially, which each should do before the court of their place of residence.

Konrad Flar, Ammann of the city of Konstanz, informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the citizen of St. Gallen Paul Brendler has handed him a sealed debt instrument dated 21 January 1492 for the 27 gulden that the apothecary Philipp of Konstanz owed him. According to a judgment that the apothecary Philipp produced, this debt instrument is invalid, whereby Brendler has defrauded him. Konrad Flar has accordingly reported this to the imperial fiscal. He asks the people of St. Gallen to hold Brendler.

Burgomaster and Council of Lindau report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the citizen of Lindau Josef Koet had sent his servant with several pieces of linen to St. Gallen to have them inspected. When the servant was asked whether the linen was made in the manner of St. Gallen, he answered yes, whereupon the linen was taken from him. The Lindauers point out that the servant may have answered out of fear or ignorance and that they had previously inquired of both the St. Galleners and the Lindauers whether they would allow linen to be inspected. They ask the St. Galleners to return the linen to the servant. They ask for a written answer with the messenger.

Hans Brendler and his wife Barbara Lehmann as well as her brother Ulrich Lehmann, citizens of St. Gallen, declare that Barbara's and Ulrichs brother Heinrich Lehmann owes them 44 gulden, two schilling and six pfennig from the inheritance of their mother. Barbara and Ursula Lehmann, the widow of Ludwig Vogelweider, in turn owe Heinrich ten gulden. Heinrich paid 34 gulden, two schilling and six pfennig, whereby the debts are settled. Hans Brendler and Ulrich Lehmann seal the document.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen write to Burgomaster and Council of Ulm that Lukas Falk, son of the carpenter Lukas Falk, citizen of St. Gallen, and cousin of the long-serving foreman Matthias Falk, wishes to inspect the damaged church in Ulm to see whether he could repair it. The St. Gallen ask the Ulm to comply with this request, to hear his opinion, and, if they agreed, to award Falk the contract for the repair.

Burkhard Schenk von Kastel, bailiff of Arbon, reports to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen how he had the citizen of St. Gallen Stefan Huld brought before the city court in St. Gallen by a proxy in order to collect an outstanding interest. Huld was sentenced to pay the interest and the expenses incurred by the proxy, but maintains that he must pay the money in St. Gallen. Although Burkhard complied with this, he did not receive the money. He therefore asks the St. Gallen authorities to confirm his rights.

Schultheiss and Council of Wil report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that their parish priest Konrad Rösch and his sister Wibrat, widow of the St. Gallen citizen Konrad Seiler, are in a legal dispute with the latter's relatives over inheritance disputes. Since Seiler's relatives are dragging out the matter, the people of Wil ask the people of St. Gallen to ensure that Konrad and Wibrat receive their rights in accordance with the existing deed of authority.

Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have set a court day for 3 December in the dispute between the Minckwitz and the Meusebach on the one hand and Daniel Kapfmann and the St. Gallen bailiff Walter Kuchimeister on the other hand, and ask the St. Gallen to announce this to their people.

Hans Billing von Esslingen, citizen of St. Gallen, reports to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he has heard that he has fallen into their disfavor due to malicious slander. He requests the written and sealed assurance of safe conduct so that he can prove his innocence.

Augustinus, organ builder in Landsberg, asks Burgomaster Hans Rainsperg and the Council of St. Gallen to grant him the commission to build the new organ in the St. Laurenzen town church. He writes that he will do the work for half the price that any other organ builder names, and names Herr Sebastian, chamberlain of the Lords of Wessobrunn, as a reference.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the King of Frankreich wishes to conquer the Kingdom of Neapel, for which reason he has hired German captains who are to recruit mercenaries in the Confederation. This is opposed by the Confederate cantons, which is why the Zürichers ask the St. Galleners to take these captains prisoner, should they encounter them, and not to permit the mercenary service.

Ludwig Ammann, town clerk of Zürich, asks Rudolf Schlaipfer, treasurer of St. Gallen, to ensure that he receives the annual interest of 25 gulden, which would have been due on 23 April. Ludwig wonders why it takes so long this year.

Burgomaster and Council of Memmingen write to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, saying that their cloth press has defects and that they are therefore sending Josef Eberli, their foreman and the bearer of this letter, to St. Gallen so that he can inspect their cloth press. They ask that he be allowed to inspect it.

Ammann and Council of Uri write to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, saying that their fields, meadows, and crops are infested with pests which they have not been able to get rid of so far. The Uri people have heard that the people of St. Gallen have a remedy against these pests, and ask them to show this to their messenger, who presents this letter, or, if this is not true, to inform them with the same messenger whether they have further information.

Konrad Kobler von Tettnang informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he has heard that the citizen of St. Gallen Franz Hutter is spreading that he wants to stab him. He asks the people of St. Gallen not to believe these accusations, and furthermore offers that Franz Hutter may seek justice before his lord Ulrich, Count von Montfort-Tettnang.

Burgomaster and Council of Isny inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that a former women's innkeeper from Kempten is staying in St. Gallen. He says that this man, together with his companions, robbed the servant who presents this letter in an inn during the fair on 23 April, for which the authorities of Isny now wanted to punish him, but so far without success. They therefore send the robbed servant to the St. Gallens so that he can describe the incident to them, and ask them to punish the women's innkeeper and his companions.

Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the Lords of Sonnenberg and Truchsessen of Waldburg rejected the agreement with the city of Ravensburg, which came about through the mediation of Rastboten from St. Gallen, Überlingen, Lindau, Wangen, Buchhorn and Konstanz, which is why the Konstanzer were asked to set a new court day, which is to take place on 30 June in Konstanz. The Konstanzer ask the St. Gallen to send their Council delegation together with those of the other cities to the court day in Konstanz. They ask for a written answer with the messenger.
Compilation of the costs incurred by the captivity of Ambrosius Spengler with the Counts of Kronberg.

Hans Kiel, Unterschreiber von Luzern, informs Hans Schenkli, town clerk of St. Gallen, that he, after having asked the St. Gallen for a coat-of-arms window and not having received it despite a promise, had commissioned such a window at his own expense and hung it among those of the other Confederates. He asks for the reimbursement of the sum of four gulden and three kreuzer that he had expended for it.

Rudolf Stucki von Mels informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he jointly with the deceased Hans Schomon von Mels stood surety for a life annuity in the amount of 17 gulden, which Abbot Ludwig Lehmann of the Benedictine abbey of Pfäfers sold. Since Lehmann is now deceased, Stucki asks the St. Gallen authorities to support him in obtaining the corresponding document from Lehmann's heirs, so that he may no longer be pursued on account of the surety.

Ulrich Lehner von Appenzell thanks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for their help in settling a dispute concerning a manslaughter, and asks them to continue supporting him. Furthermore, he wishes to present to the citizens of St. Gallen in person that he owes no one anything, even though there are people who claim otherwise.

Burgomaster and Council of Lindau inform the Council messengers of the Confederation assembled in Luzern that, in the matter between those of Appenzell and Hermann Schwendiner, they had acted upon the request of the royal Chamber Court, but had not received a copy of a corresponding letter. Furthermore, the Lindauers wish not to be troubled with such matters in the future.

Hans Lutzmann von Schwyz, bailiff at Windegg, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to hear Meister Georg Rot von Schnittlingen, bell founder, the bearer of this letter of recommendation. Jörg Rot had recently made a well-sounding bell at Weesen, which several citizens of St. Gallen had heard.

Hugo von Hohenlandenberg, Bishop of Konstanz, informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he is willing to support them in the settlement of the current dispute and approves their request not to have the matter heard before an ecclesiastical court at the moment. He asks for the names of the accused and further information about the matter.

Hugo von Hohenlandenberg, Bishop of Konstanz, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to hear Ritter Ludwig von Helmsdorf, bailiff of Bischofszell, Walter von Hallwyl, steward, and Burkhard Schenk, bailiff of Arbon, and to grant them faith in his stead.

Burgomaster and Council of Überlingen inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the citizen of St. Gallen Hans Dietz has erected a roof over a door of the parish church St. Nikolaus. This roof exhibits several defects which Dietz has not remedied despite written request, although he had given the church wardens a guarantee to remedy defects. The Überlingen representatives ask, on behalf of their church wardens, Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to approach their roofer so that he fulfills his obligation. They also ask for a written answer with the messenger.

Schultheiss and Council of Frauenfeld inform Leonhard Merz, Burgomaster of St. Gallen, that they have understood the St. Gallen response concerning the powder, and ask him to make a detour to Frauenfeld upon his return from the Diet in Luzern for an inspection concerning the powder and other matters.

Johannes Schürpf reminds the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that there is an agreement between them and him, whereby he has three to four years to study for the Doctorate in Medicine in Basel. In this regard, he made an arrangement with Meister Simon, whereby the latter received a position in St. Gallen as Schürpf's deputy as schoolmaster, over which he was very happy. However, Meister Simon did not adhere to their arrangement; instead of the promised 60 gulden for three years, Schürpf received only 30, whereby he and his family fell into distress and he could not complete his studies in three years. Johannes Schürpf therefore wishes to know whether the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen will adhere to their agreement and whether they wish to keep Meister Simon next year or whether he should procure another schoolmaster for them. If Simon is to remain, Schürpf demands from him more than the ten gulden he has received from him each year so far. If the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen do not support the agreement made between him and Simon, Schürpf renounces the position as schoolmaster and will do what is best for him and his children. He asks for a written answer, which the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen are to hand over to his cousin Jakob.

The Council messengers of the Confederates assembled in Luzern inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have received their letter concerning the soldiers who perished in Neapel and that they have allowed all soldiers to petition the King of Frankreich so that justice be done for all those affected. The King's reply is to be sent to Luzern so that all members of the Confederation are informed.

Konrad Hirt, Licentiate of Ecclesiastical Law, informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that, on their advice and command, he had spoken to Master Johannes Oderbolz in Freiburg regarding the parish priesthood. The latter told him that he would shortly communicate to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, orally or in writing, his decision as to whether he himself or another would be provided with his benefice. Since the citizens of St. Gallen had promised Hirt the parish priesthood, he now asks for further advice.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they had asked their citizen Rudolf Hedinger in writing to speak with Philipp Fechter of Lyon, who asserts claims against several citizens of St. Gallen and wishes to enforce them by official authority. Hedinger informs the citizens of Zürich that Fechter intends to stand by his claims. Furthermore, Hedinger is not travelling to the court of the French King, and his companions had set out and returned to him in Lyon before the letter from Zürich arrived.

Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that, because of the dispute between the St. Gallen citizen Rudolf Schläpfer and Varnbüler over interest and property in Sipplingen, they had sent their own messenger to Sipplingen, where Daniel Spengler, Varnbüler's attorney, had seized Schläpfer's property. The judges would not yet know how this dispute should be decided, but it might possibly be adjudicated before the King or before the Imperial Chamber Court. The St. Gallen messenger waited in the meantime in Konstanz.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen inform Burgomaster and Council of Zürich that their town clerk reported to them on a Diet resolution in Luzern and a new day set for the coming Wednesday in Zürich. Because of serious unrest in several places, they have equipped additional mercenaries under a banner in addition to the troops stationed at Rheineck and have armed themselves with additional levies. The St. Gallen send their messenger and ask the Zürcher to inform them of the decisions made at the day in Zürich.

The Council messengers of the cities and lands of the Confederation, assembled in Basel, inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they had conducted peace negotiations with the royal councillors and lawyers and that a further day has been set, to which they are to appear in the inn in Schaffhausen on Wednesday evening, 4 September. Until then, a truce is to prevail. The St. Gallen Council messengers will later report in detail on the day.

The Council messengers of the lands and towns of the Confederation, assembled in Basel, inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have determined that they each have different instructions regarding the articles of the agreement that is to end the war with the King, while Uri and Glarus have not sent any Council messengers at all. Since in particular the Associated Cantons are war-weary, they wish to be content with the Landgericht in Thurgau, as Konstanz holds it, and to renounce the courts in the Prättigau, possibly Tiengen, Küssaberg, and in the Klettgau. Furthermore, the members of the Empire are prepared for a longer war, and a Confederate victory is by no means certain, even with the help of the French cannons. Conquests by the Confederates would rather provoke the opposing party and strengthen resistance. Therefore, the Milanese mediators were sent to the King to find out whether peace is possible under these conditions. The truce is to be extended until 16 September, so that the Milanese mediators have time until then to receive an answer from the King. In the event that no peace should come about, the Confederates plan an attack on Gottlieben and subsequently Bregenz and Feldkirch, and ask the St. Gallen to send their troops to Gottlieben on 19 September. They ask the St. Gallen to equip their Council message with powers of attorney so that the negotiations can continue.

Burgomaster and Council of Buchhorn inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have sent their Gredmeister to the Landvogt to ensure that the goods coming from St. Gallen to Buchhorn are protected. Since the Landvogt was in Ulm, the Gredmeister sought out the representatives of the Landvogt, who promised him the protection of the goods. As a precaution, a delegation was nevertheless sent to Ulm to obtain a definitive answer from the Landvogt. The people of Buchhorn want to inform the people of St. Gallen as soon as this answer reaches them.

Galeazzo, ducal vice-count, writes to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, saying that he had learned through the citizen of St. Gallen Gilg that Stefan and Hans Grübel as well as Herli Ritz, who had supplied him with mercenaries as captains, had fallen into disgrace. He asks the people of St. Gallen to pardon them.

Daniel Kapfmann urgently asks Johannes Schenkli, town clerk of St. Gallen, to intervene on his behalf, whether with the rulers in Mailand or with the King, so that he may obtain his right, and offers him purple in return.

Burgomaster and Council of Chur inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that, in accordance with their agreement in the dispute between Benedikt Burgauer and his wife, they sent her money to him. However, it is less money than is mentioned in the agreement of the St. Gallen, as it is to be assumed that Burgauer has invested his money in interest and therefore it is no longer available. The Chur ask the St. Gallen to ensure that the agreement is upheld and that the wife and children of Burgauer are protected from him.

Schultheiss and Council of Wil request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, in the name of the Wil councilor Hans Sailer and their servant Hans Grossmann, to compel the St. Gallen citizen Bernhard Bühler to fulfill his written obligations to the citizens of Wil. He has not yet arrived in Wil, although he had promised to do so.

Ammann, Council and Community of Uri inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the King of Frankreich has not kept the promises he made to the recruited soldiers, whereby the Urians feel their honor injured. The Urians therefore plan a march for Saturday 11 September and ask the St. Gallen for support.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request the Council envoys of the cities and lands of the Confederation assembled in Luzern, Hans Ammann and Mennli Kunz, who are to show this letter, to recognize, in the pending negotiation of an Obmann, the claims against the French King as representatives of the survivors of those men who fell in French service in Neapel and Kalabrien, even if some documents may be missing.

Lukas Falk, master builder of St. Gallen, informs the St. Gallen Council messengers assembled at the Diet in Luzern that he will soon be finished with his work in Uri. He wishes to know when he is expected back in St. Gallen, as he still has something to attend to. He asks for a written reply with the bearer of this letter as to when they would need him in St. Gallen. Furthermore, he has heard that the Schwyzers wish to build a new bridge, and he asks the St. Gallen for their intercession for this commission with the Schwyz Council messengers, who are also at the Diet.

Knight Ludwig von Helmsdorf, bailiff of Bischofszell, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to support the citizen Dorothea Tennenberg, the widow of the farrier Heinrich Rietmann, and her bailiff, Kleinhans Schneider, who present this letter. The citizen of St. Gallen Ulrich Betz had promised the deceased husband Heinrich Rietmann the money for the apprenticeship of his son. However, the payment was not made. Dorothea had also made the offer that the boy could work off the apprenticeship fee, but he had secretly run away along with his clothes. Helmsdorf asks the St. Gallen authorities to ensure that Dorothea receives the outstanding money for the apprenticeship of her son from Ulrich Betz, or, if Betz has objections, that the case be dealt with.

Burgomaster and Council of Ulm report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that in their city, on the last Tuesday morning, 11 May, a mutilated body of a powerfully built man was found. This is possibly an executioner from the Lake Constance region or from the Confederation, who came to Ulm around Christmas. The Ulm ask the St. Gallen to inquire whether an executioner is missing and what he looked like and what he had been wearing. They ask for a written reply with this messenger.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that, following an attack on two citizens of St. Gallen between Radolfzell and Allensbach and their abduction by Wolf, Adam, Heinrich Sigmund and Wolfdietrich von Homburg, they have received a letter in which these men tell them that their brother and their cousin are in a dispute with the Confederates, but that they themselves do not wish to take part in it. The Zürcher also learned from the Abbot of the monastery of Reichenau, in whose territory the attack took place, that he knows nothing about it. The same applies to the Lords of Friedingen on Hohenkrähen. Furthermore, they have learned from the Council delegation of Stein am Rhein that the Lords of Klingenberger on Hohentwiel also know nothing and regret the attack, especially as they are interested in a good relationship with the Confederates. The Zürcher intend to advocate for the St. Gallen at the upcoming Diet in Luzern.

Burgomaster and Council of Überlingen assure Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they will try to find out who attacked and abducted the citizens of St. Gallen. Should any indignities befall visitors from St. Gallen at the Überlingen market, within or outside the city, the Überlingen authorities ask the St. Gallen authorities to inform them thereof.

Hieronymus Stocker von Zug, Landvogt in Thurgau, informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that messengers from Zihlschlacht told him that they demanded levies from three farms of the Hospital of St. Gallen on account of the past war, as they would also do with other farms in their community. The hospital master defends himself against this by referring to an agreement with the Welter of Blidegg, who is to cover this. Stocker asks the St. Gallen, in the name of the Confederates, to support the hospital master in this matter so that the hospital master pays the levies, as otherwise the community might take by force what is due to it.

The Küster and chapter of the Stift at Markdorf ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to consider Michael Altherr of St. Gallen, who has conducted himself as a model holder of a prebend of a canon, for the vacant position as Kaplan in St. Gallen. The request to the St. Gallen authorities is made at the behest of Altherr to the Küster and the chapter of the Stift.

Klaus Beiger, citizen of Rottweil, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to send the annual interest in the amount of 15 gulden, which the citizens of St. Gallen are in debt on 25 December, to Heinrich Rottengatters house in Konstanz, where they will receive a receipt for it.

Burgomaster and Council of Lindau inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they will send a Council delegation to the Emperor to have their freedoms confirmed and to advocate for further Lindau matters. The Council messenger will be ready to travel in five to six days. The Lindauers offer the St. Galleners that their Council delegation will also advocate for the St. Galleners, if there are matters they wish to present to the Emperor.

Ulrich Kuhn, Werkmeister in Bischofszell and citizen of St. Gallen, informs Burgomaster Johannes Schenkli of St. Gallen that he has heard that the Werkmeister of St. Gallen intends to leave. Since his citizenship was extended until the next Christmas, he asks the Burgomaster to find out what the Werkmeister intends to do and to inform him about it. Furthermore, Ulrich asks for the Burgomaster's support in the event that the position of Werkmeister becomes vacant.

Statthalter and Council of St. Gallen inform Burgomaster Johannes Schenkli and Imperial Bailiff Leonhard Merz, who are staying in Baden at a Diet, that they had learned from the Landweibel of Appenzell that several Appenzeller servants and Gotteshausleute of St. Gallen had gone to the Margrave of Brandenburg to march against Nürnberg. The Landweibel wishes to learn from the St. Gallen people what they will undertake in view of the consequences this may have for the surroundings. The St. Gallen people have just publicly forbidden military service under penalty to honor, body, and property, and the Prince-Abbot is likewise of this opinion. The Landweibel will inform the Appenzeller authority about this, and Schenkli and Merz are to report this to the other Confederate council envoys in Baden if necessary.

Ambrosius Eigen in Mailand informs Burgomaster Johannes Schenkli of St. Gallen that he has spoken with Beeli about the annual payment. He says that the latter has not been at court for three years, where the agreement was concluded, but has been in Lombardei. Eigen handed Beeli the receipt and learned that the servants are to go to Genua and from there to Neapel. Beeli promised to advocate for the citizens of St. Gallen with the King, who is still in Asti in Piemont, as soon as the latter comes to Mailand. Eigen will endeavor to ensure that the servants of St. Gallen receive their money, and he asks that a messenger be made available to Beeli.

The Councils of the Confederation assembled in Baden thank the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for accepting the settlement in a dispute. The Council messengers of the Confederates have furthermore issued an ordinance against mercenary service and the pension system, which they enclose. They ask the St. Gallen authorities to deliberate on it, in order to adopt it at the future Diet in Baden together with the St. Gallen delegation.

Gallus Bils, schoolmaster in Wangen, informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he has learned that their school has no schoolmaster. He asks the St. Gallen authorities to consider him for this position. Should the St. Gallen authorities not want him, he asks them to keep his letter secret so that it does not harm him in his current position.

The Councils of the cities and lands of the Confederation, assembled in Baden, inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the sworn renewal of the alliances is approaching, which is why the St. Gallen Council envoys are to arrive at the inn on 5 July in order to carry out the renewal of the alliances the following day, on Tuesday 6 July.

Schultheiss and Council of Wil report in haste to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they had learned from the bailiff of Schwarzenbach that a man with red trousers and a black coat, who had asked for directions, had reported a fire in St. Gallen. The men of Wil had thereupon questioned the man, who carried two letters with him that had been entrusted to him by Paul Brennler. The men of Wil send the letters and ask for a written or oral message with this messenger on how they are to conduct themselves, as they had become suspicious and had interrogated and taken the man into custody.

Erasmus Riff, called Welter von Blidegg, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to permit his cousin Ludwig Welter, bailiff of Güttingen, who wishes to conduct the dispute with his brother-in-law Hans Wiler before the court of Philipp, Pfalzgraf bei Rhein, in Germersheim, to make use of the services of Doctor Mangolt and to make him ready to travel.

Schultheiss and Council of Bern inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they are grateful that the St. Gallen citizens wish to warn against forged roll batzen, which are issued from St. Gallen, Solothurn and Bern. They inform the St. Gallen citizens that they have received letters accusing Johann Darrax Pernet and his wife Johanna from Gex near Genf, and that they have been taken prisoner. He stated that the coins were struck by a Grand Sandrin from Brabant and Hennegau, who lives near Strassburg, and handed over to him. The Bernese ask the St. Gallen citizens to inquire with the rulers in Maastricht and other places about the originator of the coin forgery, who had been reported to them, and to interrogate the prisoner.

The Councils of the cities and lands of the Confederation, assembled in Zürich, inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that, on account of the mercenaries in French and papal service and on account of the Pope, Frankreich, and Venedig, who all wish to make an agreement with the Confederates, they have appointed a day for 12 June in Luzern. They ask the St. Gallen to send an empowered embassy.

Knight Hans von Landau, Imperial Treasurer, informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the jubilee funds, which were decreed by Pope Alexander, are due. The Emperor has commissioned him with the collection, but he is prevented by other business. Instead, he sends his brother-in-law Moritz von Altmannshofen, and he asks the citizens of St. Gallen to hand over the money to him against a receipt.

The Councils of the cities and lands of the Confederation assembled in Baden inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that their envoys from Mailand, who had obtained cannons there for the bombardment of Lugano, have returned. Thereupon, they had ordered the gunners to proceed thither to bombard the castle. However, these now report that they have too little powder. The Councils of the Confederates therefore wish to know whether St. Gallen has the necessary quantity or can manufacture it in the city, and what that costs; they would pay in cash. If they could not manufacture powder, the St. Gallen citizens should give their own. They ask for an answer with the same messenger.

Urban Hegenwald, Münzer, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to ensure that he finally receives his money, as they had assured him in writing, since he has fallen into great distress because of the delay. He asks for the repayment of the principal sum and compensation.

Schultheiss and Council of Luzern ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to report to them what they have learned from the arrested Ambrosius about the persons who intend to march against the Confederates in Mailand for the French King, as this causes unrest in the land. They ask for immediate communication of the statements of Ambrosius and other relevant information with the same messenger.

Statthalter and Council of Schwyz inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen in haste that they have learned from the messengers to Mailand and the soldiers in the Feld that the French King will invade Mailand at three places and that the Confederate soldiers intend to march against him. Thereupon a day was set in Beckenried, where it was decided to send further men to the south for support. The Urner will march out on 16 April and the Schwyzer on 17 April to assemble the troops in Vercelli. They ask the St. Gallen to announce this also to the Prince-Abbot.

Schultheiss and Council of Bern inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that, at the request of the French King and his lawyers, they have convened a day for 20 January in Bern to discuss and, if possible, seal the Peace of Genf. The day already set for the same date in Luzern is to be postponed. The Bernese ask the St. Gallen to send a delegation.

Emperor Maximilian informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that his servant Hans Flächsner reported to him that no decision had yet been reached in the legal dispute with Bernhard Flachsner, a citizen of St. Gallen, called Ani, and that he had incurred great expenses. Therefore, Flächsener had now requested the Emperor's support. Emperor Maximilian urges the citizens of St. Gallen to make every effort to settle the dispute as quickly as possible.

The Councils of the six Confederate cantons Zürich, Zug, Basel, Solothurn, Schaffhausen and Appenzell, assembled in Zürich, as well as Prince-Abbot Franz Gaisberg of St. Gallen, send the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen a farewell from the Diet, which they have just concluded, and ask them to send their empowered envoys on the day decided upon in the farewell.
The Duke of Württemberg and the 11 Confederate cantons fear an uprising and ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for assistance to prevent it.

Council messengers from Zürich, Luzern, Zug and Glarus address the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen. They report on a conflict concerning the high jurisdiction in Oberneunforn between the nine cantons, which share in the Landgrafschaft in Thurgau, on the one hand and Zürich on the other, and that they have chosen an Obmann, namely the St. Gallen Säckelmeister Keller, for mediation.
Six Confederate cantons ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for legal assistance in the case of the killing of Klaus Bruder of St. Gallen, committed by Ulrich Schmuckli of Schmucklisberg.

Schultheiss and Council of Solothurn report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that a citizen of St. Gallen had brought letters addressed to the knight Dietrich von Schauenburg. As this dispatch of letters aroused mistrust, they had ascertained from the messenger that the letters had been handed to him by the St. Gallen town ammann Tristan Studer. After the Solothurners saw that the letters were addressed to the French king and other French lords, they had confiscated them and delivered them to the French attorney in Bern.

Schultheiss and Council of Bern request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to send an authorized Council delegation to Luzern on 20 March to a Confederate consultation. The request of the French King for more mercenaries is to be dealt with.

The Council envoys of the Confederation assembled in Baden write to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, saying that a heretic named Krüsi, whom the St. Gallen had taken prisoner for heretical preaching and had released again against a pledge of peace, continues to preach in St. Georgen. They ask the St. Gallen to observe the man and to punish him for perjury and unchristian conduct.

The council envoys of the 12 cantons of the Confederation, assembled in Luzern, complain to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the Lutheran, devilish heresy prevailing in St. Gallen. They admonish the citizens of St. Gallen to act against it and to uphold the holy Mass. They expect a written or oral answer with the messenger to the next Confederate assembly, which will take place on 14 September in Baden.

Burgomaster and Council of Thun address Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen regarding warlike actions with the Duke of Mailand on behalf of the Drei Bünde. They have sent their fellow citizen Michel Burgauer to St. Gallen with the commission to procure gunpowder and ask for support.
Burgomaster and Council of Zürich thank Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for a letter. They assure them of their loyal friendship.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich address Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen with the communication that they have been informed that some cantons did not want to renew the Confederation with those who did not want to remain in the old faith. The citizens of Zürich assure the citizens of St. Gallen that they wanted to maintain the Confederation with them as before, which they also hoped from the citizens of St. Gallen towards them.

Ammann and Council of Schwyz address themselves, on behalf of Adrion Fischli, the guardian of the widow Katherina Reutlinger, citizen of St. Gallen and now resident (Hintersasse) in Schwyz, to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen with the request to ensure that her property, which was seized by St. Gallen, be released again. She has namely settled the debts of her deceased husband. Schwyz asks for an answer with the same messenger.

Zehn Council messengers of the Confederate cantons gathered in Baden ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to provide assistance from the hospital to Ulrich Schweizer, who had been in a legal dispute with the deceased St. Gallen hospital master in Lustenau and to whom the Landvogt of Rheineck had forbidden access to the court in Lustenau.
Colonel Georg Göldli, commander of the Zürich contingent, reports to the Burgomaster and Council of Zürich in the main letter and the enclosure on the current situation in the Second Müsser War.

The enclosure concerns the Second Müsser War. After the Bündner asked the Confederates for help, Zürich, Bern, Glarus, the County of Toggenburg, the Thurgau, Solothurn, Freiburg, Basel, Schaffhausen and Appenzell sent troops and cannons to Chur.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich repeatedly, urgently, and in the greatest haste call upon Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to come to their aid immediately with troops of St. Gallen in the Kappelerkrieg.

Burgomaster, Council and citizens of Zürich report in haste to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about their departure for Bremgarten. They say that they had allowed the Rheintalers to stay at home, but now ask the St. Gallen to lend them several halberds.

Diethelm Blarer von Wartensee, abbot of the Benedictine monastery of St. Gallen, demands, on the basis of the peace of the Confederation, that the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen return all property and rights of the monastery which the city has temporarily and unlawfully appropriated. Should they not comply with this demand, the abbot says that he will seek help. He asks for a written answer with the same messenger.

Erasmus Lenggenhager asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for support regarding his engagement lawsuit pending before the marriage court against Dorothea, daughter of Jakob Zollikofer. Lenggenhager insists on the validity of the engagement and intends to appeal against an already issued judgment. As he must travel for business, he intends to file the appeal after his return. In the meantime, Dorothea must not enter into any other marriage negotiations.

Burgomaster and Council of Ulm request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to observe the attached coinage ordinance in order to combat the great damage caused by the variety of coinage and to promote the common good.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich write to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, as their citizen Melchior Iselin was sold an unsealed Zwilch by the St. Gallen Gabriel Billwiler at the market in Zurzach. The St. Gallen seller claims that the sealing had been forgotten. As the St. Gallen authorities wish to clarify the matter, they ask the Zürich authorities for the delivery of this Zwilch or a piece of it.

Statthalter and Council of Appenzell ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for legal assistance. It concerns the punishment of Gallus Brissig, who is suspected of having killed his wife. They ask for the arrest of Gallus Brissig as soon as he leaves the area of freedom.

Burgomaster and Council of Kempten address Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen on behalf of their citizen Oswald Merz regarding an inheritance dispute. They ask the St. Gallen authorities to seize an inheritance share already paid out to the St. Gallen citizen Ulrich Sailer, until a court hearing conducted by Kempten has decided whether their citizen Merz is also entitled to the inheritance in this matter or not. The Kempten authorities request the delivery of a written reply through their resident Heinrich Graf, the bearer of this letter.

Burgomaster and Council of Rottweil address, in the name of Anna Armbruster, Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen. About five years ago, the now deceased citizen of Rottweil, Hans Vorster, had taken in two orphaned children from his brother-in-law Ulrich Girtanner and his sister with 80 gulden to raise them. After the death of Hans Vorster, his surviving wife, named Anna Armbruster, had married another man, who, however, left her because of military service. Anna Armbruster now asks to be allowed to take in the orphaned children in addition to her two other children, and to be granted the 60 gulden remaining from the 80 for the maintenance of the children.

The Vice-Statthalter of the King and Regent of the Upper Austrian lands Ferdinand I. informs the city of St. Gallen about a coinage ordinance concluded between Basel, Freiburg im Breisgau, Colmar, Breisach and Thann, to refrain from the minting of batzen in the future. However, batzen of these cities already struck will continue to be traded at the value of four kreuzer.

King Ferdinand I. sends to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen a copy of a letter submitted to him by Friedrich Pfalzgraf bei Rhein, the Bishop of Bamberg Weigand von Redwitz, Margrave Georg the Pious of Brandenburg-Ansbach, Landgrave Georg of Leuchtenberg, and the Burgomaster and Council of Nürnberg, in which they communicate to the King their opinion on the new coinage ordinance agreed upon in Ingolstadt. The King convenes a consultation in Augsburg on 26 March and calls upon the St. Gallen to send an embassy.

Friedrich Pfalzgraf bei Rhein, the Bishop of Bamberg Weigand von Redwitz, Margrave Georg der Fromme von Brandenburg-Ansbach, Landgraf Georg von Leuchtenberg and Burgomaster and Council of Nürnberg communicate to the King their opinion on the new coinage order. They ask the King for a reply.

Burgomaster Adelberg Meyer and Council of Basel request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to send a Council delegation to Basel on Sunday, 26. March. On Monday 27. March, together with other co-believers of the Confederation, they are to continue deliberating on the confessional question and finally reach a decision.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to send a Council delegation to Aarau on 18 April. It is to be deliberated how to proceed with the bandits detained in Bern and how the disputes are to be settled. In addition, the Zürcher send the St. Gallen the report on questions of confession received from Basel concerning the Diet of the Imperial Estates and the Emperor at Augsburg. The Zürcher ask to be informed how a reply should be given in this regard.

The Dreizehner Rat of Strassburg asks the Council of Basel for a meeting to reach an agreement on the question of the Sacrament. Martin Luther wished for a meeting, and Martin Butzer sought the appropriate time and place for it. The meeting is to take place on 14 May in Eisenach. It is suggested to invite further Reformers such as Vadian, Capito, Bullinger and others.

The Statthalter of the Burgomaster's Office and Council of Basel write to the Burgomaster and Council of Zürich that they would send a Council delegation with several preachers on the coming Friday, 11 August, to report on the meeting with Martin Luther. They inform the citizens of Zürich that Vadian, Burgomaster of St. Gallen, was also to participate.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich, against the background of rumors of new enlistments into foreign service, urgently urge Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen as well as the other Confederate cantons to consistently enforce the ban on mercenary service. The occasion is in particular the case of bailiff Schönbrunner, from whom horses and property were confiscated due to the unauthorized recruitment of Confederate soldiers. Zürich reaffirms its firm will to fundamentally prevent foreign pensions, pay, and recruitment, and calls on the Confederate authorities to dismiss, punish, if necessary imprison, and confiscate the property of those who violate this.

Burgomaster Jakob Meyer and the Council of Basel inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the deliberation of the Protestants in Schmalkalden regarding participation in a council planned by Pope Paulus for the coming May in Mantua. Several copies of various letters are attached to the letter. The Basel authorities ask the St. Gallen authorities to study the letters with regard to a future meeting.

Philipp Melanchthon informs, on behalf of Johann Friedrich, Elector of Sachsen, the Burgomasters, Schultheiss and Councils of Zürich, Bern, Basel, Schaffhausen, St. Gallen, Mühlhausen and Biel, that Martin Luther has not answered their letter because he is ill. He says that he will answer them in detail as soon as he is well.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich send Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen a printed letter, addressed to Pope Paul III., issued by Johann Friedrich, Duke and Elector of Sachsen, and Philipp, Landgrave of Hessen, as well as other Princes and Estates, for their information.

The Council envoys of the 12 cantons of the Confederation assembled in Baden write to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they should pursue Kaspar Guggi only in Appenzell. It is customary that the canton and court where a person is resident have jurisdiction, and Guggi has pledged obedience to the Appenzellers. The Landvogt of Baden and Bannerlord Andreas Schmid as well as the Council of Zürich seal it.

Burgomaster and Council of Rottweil report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen on the assets and inheritance conditions of the minor children of the deceased Ulrich Girtanner from his marriage with the likewise deceased Barbara Vorster. After the death of both parents as well as other relatives, parts of the estate were sold to settle debts, so that only 80 gulden remained for the children. This sum was initially handed over to the uncle Hanns Vorster the Younger for fiduciary administration, who, however, also died. Due to the danger of loss of assets, the parties involved, with the participation of the St. Gallen bailiff Albrecht Rieger, agreed that 60 gulden be paid out to the children and that they be sent to their relatives in St. Gallen. Rottweil declares itself willing to keep the children in the citizenship, provided that the annual dues are paid, and refers to Lorenz Findenschatz, Girtanner's former business partner, for any further assets.

The Strasbourg reformers Wolfgang Capito and Martin Butzer write to the Confederate cities of Zürich, Bern, Basel, Schaffhausen, St. Gallen, Mülhausen and Biel. The letter begins with a copy of the answer from Martin Luther to a letter concerning the Concord. It concerns the differing understanding of the Lord's Supper and the agreement reached. Capito and Butzer then take a position on Luther's answer as well as on the understanding of the Lord's Supper and report on the negotiations.

Dissatisfied citizens of St. Gallen address a libel and complaint document to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen. Johann Valentin Furtmüller stirs up unrest in the city. He slanders citizens and guild masters, competes with city artisans through his Ämter who would be glad to have city Ämter, preaches lies, attracts other litigants, and wants to incite an overthrow. The Burgomaster and Council should forbid him from preaching and expel him from the city. The citizens demand that city Ämter in the future should only be filled with citizens. Furthermore, they complain about wage cuts for officials, bans on dancing and games, unequal treatment of rich and poor citizens in the judiciary, about deficiencies in poor relief and in the school system, as well as about the abuse of power by some families in the Council. Accusations of nepotism among the ruling families are raised. The dissatisfied citizens warn of an uprising.

Johannes Gebendinger writes to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, saying that he has been informed that he is being slandered for having written a libel against them, and that they intend to arrest him. He therefore went to Konstanz to seek advice, then returned to his wife, who reported to him that he had already been sought out by the city watchmen. He repeatedly emphasizes that he is innocent and asks to be allowed to defend himself. To avoid arrest, he has fled, from where he writes in haste.

Ammann and Council of Appenzell report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about an inquiry conducted in a dispute over a payment claim, in which the citizen of St. Gallen Peter Rugensperger is involved. Ammann and Council of Appenzell interrogate their resident Peter Unger and his wife Elsa Tobler as witnesses. At Rugensperger's request, the Appenzellers certify the matter and authenticate this letter with their secret seal.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich send to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen a copy of the answers of the Princes of Sachsen and Hessen as well as Martin Luther to the letter sent by the citizens of Zürich and St. Gallen to them.

Burgomaster and Council of Basel send Burgomaster and Council of Zürich a copy of a letter from the Dreizehner Rat (Kriegsverordnete) of Strassburg. Since the Baselers wish to promote an agreement with Martin Luther, and since they assume that this is also in the sense of the Zürchers and of other members of the same religion, they ask Zürich, Schaffhausen and St. Gallen to report on the letter. They have already written to Bern. They ask the Zürchers to inform their sent messenger how the matter is to be handled and whether they also considered a meeting necessary.

The Dreizehner Rat (Kriegsverordneten) of Strassburg informs the Burgomaster and Council of Basel about the report of the envoys who have returned from the deliberations in Eisenach. The letters to the Kurfürst of Sachsen and the Landgraf of Hessen, as well as their and Martin Luther's answers thereto, were read out, praised as exemplary Christian writings, and recommended for further dissemination. The Baselers are asked to forward this to members of the same religion in order to promote concord in the Christian doctrine. Furthermore, they report that this meeting in Eisenach was dedicated primarily to the preservation of peace, so that aid could be offered to the King in the fight against the Turks.

Landammann and Council of Appenzell write to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen regarding their countryman Kaspar Schuhmacher. They have, as requested by the St. Gallen authorities, interrogated Kaspar Schuhmacher concerning his wife Elsbeth, the daughter of the St. Gallen citizen named Bruderer. Schuhmacher is aware of his guilt, repents his actions, and asks his wife and his father-in-law for forgiveness. He wishes for his wife to return to him, which the Appenzell authorities support. The Appenzell authorities ask for a reply.

Burgomaster and Council of Basel inform Burgomaster and Council of Zürich about the disputes in Minden in Westfalen and about the judgment of the imperial Kammergericht regarding the resigned clergy. The information is intended to serve as a warning and is also to be forwarded to Burgomaster and Councils of St. Gallen and Schaffhausen. An enclosed letter from the Burgomaster, Council and Community of Minden explains the criminal complaint and the judgment.
The Burgomaster, Council and Community of Minden explain the criminal complaint and the judgment in the dispute of the city against the clergy of Minden.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich hand over to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen a copy of a farewell from the negotiations held in Frankfurt. The Zürichers have been informed by the Baselers and asked to treat the matter confidentially and to forward it. The Zürichers ask the St. Galleners to likewise inform them of any news that might be important.

King Ferdinand I. informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the date of 11 August agreed upon at the Münztag in Augsburg for a further meeting will be postponed to 24 August. The King urges the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to send their envoys to Augsburg for this date.

The 13 cantons of the Confederation assembled in Baden address the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, asking them to issue an ordinance against forward buying, as they themselves have done. Lately, Germans and Welsche have been coming into the Confederation and buying grain directly from farmers and at mills, and hoarding it. This has resulted in price increases, which affect the poor above all. It should be stipulated that goods may only be sold on the free markets. This is to prevent usurious prices and the unauthorized export of large Mengen of grain from the Confederation.

The Council messengers sent by the city of Augsburg to the Coinage Day of 24 August send as an enclosure to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen a copy of the sealed conclusion of the Coinage Day and report that they had represented the city of St. Gallen there, as requested in writing, and had excused its absence.
Copy of the aforementioned departure from the coinage day of 24 August, which was delivered as an enclosure to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich complain to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have again permitted the pension system with Frankreich. They mention the case of Franziskus Studer, who is admitted as a resident (Hintersasse) in St. Gallen and can thus engage in the pension system. Furthermore, the citizens of Zürich enclose a letter regarding the new toll levy of Frankreich.

Adelberg Meyer, Burgomaster and Council of Basel, reports to the Burgomaster and Council of Zürich that Frankreich is levying new, harmful customs duties of five percent. Basel asks for the information to be passed on to other Confederate cantons and requests that the matter be discussed in Baden.

Draft by Vadians in the name of the small and great Council of St. Gallen to the Burgomaster and Council of Zürich, in which he answers the letter from Zürich of 25. März 1540 concerning the pension matter and justifies the course of action of the St. Gallen in this regard.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen confirm to Bonifatius Spengler, citizen of St. Gallen, with a certificate his legitimate birth and his honest way of life. Spengler wishes, because he was left by his wife, to move with his small children to Bern, where he has acquaintances who would help him.

Konrad Zwick of Konstanz explains to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen the facts of a debt of money that Hans Kayser owes him, which is however also claimed by Konrad Schlappritzi and Bartholome Schuber for themselves. The disputes were heard in court. With the report on the facts, Konrad Zwick wishes to preserve his honor and his good reputation.

Burgomaster and Council of Kempten reply to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen regarding St. Gallen's inquiry about alleged threats by arsonists against the city of St. Gallen. The Kempten authorities report on fires and subsequent convictions of arsonists in Ravensburg, Kempten, Wangen, Sonthofen, Füssen and Leutkirch and the surrounding area, but deny having heard of any threats against St. Gallen. They attach to this letter a copy of the conviction of a murder-arsonist in Ravensburg and promise to immediately report any threats against St. Gallen.

Rasi Appenzeller asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to readmit him to the city. He promises to pay his debts and not to gamble anymore, and submits himself to the city's punitive authority in case of violation. In justification of his petition, he refers to damages and injuries suffered during work and assistance, among other things at the Albasberg and at the Walke on the Schorenweg, and states that he intends to collect outstanding claims in court and use them to pay off his debts.
Ammann and Community of Uttwil recommend to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to hear Christian Appenzeller, citizen of St. Gallen and preacher in Uttwil, in a matter unknown to them.

Anton Merz writes to Ulrich Hetzer, hospital master of St. Gallen, and asserts his innocence in a crime of which he is suspected. He describes in detail an interrogation by Hetzer, during which he made a false confession under pressure, although he is innocent. Merz explains that he subsequently fled with one gulden and a heavy heart, asks God for the truth to be revealed, and hopes for his vindication. He asks Hetzer to determine the true perpetrators, offers to answer for himself before his gracious lords, and requests a letter to Baden.

Burgomaster and secret councillors of Ulm request Burgomaster and secret councillors of St. Gallen to deliver up to 50 centners of saltpeter for the fight against the Turks/Ottomans. They justify this with an upcoming Imperial Diet in Speyer on 14 January 1542, at which aid against the Ottomans is to be discussed, as well as with their exhaustion of gunpowder after years of wars in Ungarn. They request written information regarding price, payment terms, and delivery via their messenger and offer cash payment.

Burgomaster and the five secret councillors of Ulm thank Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for the offer to supply at least 30 centners of saltpeter and gunpowder at the purchase price. They announce that on 2 February 1542 they will send a delegate to St. Gallen for inspection and purchase. They ask that as much saltpeter as possible be procured until his arrival, and request prior written information regarding prices and payment terms.

Burgomaster and five secret councillors of Ulm ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to inform them, regarding the purchase of saltpeter, how much a hundredweight weighs in the territory of the city of St. Gallen in comparison with Ulm.
Ambrosius Falk asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for new summer clothing (a pair of twill trousers, a doublet, and a linen shirt), so that he can perform his office in the summer.

Heinrich, Abbot of Wettingen, informs Hans Studer, Burgomaster of St. Gallen, that he will pursue Albrecht Mayer, a resident of the city of St. Gallen and former stable master, for ten gulden due to a past horse purchase. The messenger of the letter, Peter Bellotretter, is equipped with the abbot's power of attorney to collect the debts amicably or legally. Heinrich asks the Burgomaster of St. Gallen to support his proxy.

Christian Appenzeller thanks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for the grace and mercy which the authority showed him, his siblings, and his mother and which preserved them from starvation. He also asks the authority of St. Gallen not to hold the offenses of his father, Christian Appenzeller, against them and to readmit him as a citizen of the city of St. Gallen.

Statthalter and Council of Baden confirm to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen the receipt of their letter regarding the inheritance of Gallus Ruch, to which the St. Gallen citizen Wybrat Scherrer, his mother, asserts a claim. Gallus Ruch died in the hospital in Baden and left only clothes, which he bequeathed to the children of his brother, Ulrich Ruch. It is further reported that the debt claims of St. Gallen citizens against Ulrich Ruch will be considered, provided that money remains after the sale of his house and household goods.

The marriage judges of the city and territory of Zürich explain to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen their decision in the marriage dispute between Michael Bregenzer of Gossau and Verena Hunn, daughter of a citizen of St. Gallen. Contrary to the wish of the St. Gallen authorities, the couple is not divorced. Verena had complained that her man had burdened her with invented slanders and that she did not feel safe in body and life with him. She possesses a written document from Zürich for her protection. However, the Zürich court decides that, according to the articles and statutes of the Reformed cantons, no divorce is possible. Verena is to move to her husband and help him to raise the common children. Zürich obliges the bailiff of Grüningen, Hans Balthasar Keller, to see to it that Michael Bregenzer behaves righteously in the future.

Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz inform Burgomaster and secret Councillors of St. Gallen about their military support of the Schmalkaldic League against the Catholic Duke Heinrich II. von Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel in his attack on the city of Goslar and warn that in the event of an intervention by the Catholic League, these disturbances could become noticeable in the upper (southern German) lands.

Burgomaster and Council of Lindau request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for support in an inheritance matter. Their citizen Konrad Wernz von Oberreitnau is the appointed bailiff of Agatha Müller and Elisabeth Mösch, both legitimate daughters of the deceased Katharina Grublin from Humbertsweiler. Agatha Müller, daughter from Katharina's first marriage to Bartholomäus Müller, has died in St. Gallen and has left no closer heirs than her half-sister Elisabeth Mösch, daughter from Katharina's second marriage to Martin Mösch. Elisabeth is thus the only lawful heir of Agatha. Lindau asks St. Gallen to assist the bailiff so that the poor orphan may come to her lawful inheritance, and with as little cost as possible and by the quickest route.

Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the progress of the war between the Schmalkaldic League and Duke Heinrich II. von Braunschweig-Wolfenbüttel.
