Konstanz had already reported on the course of the war on 24 August. Now Konstanz reports new events: on 5 August 1542, the castle of Wolfenbüttel was surrendered. It is further reported that the opponents were allowed to withdraw and that troops of the Schmalkaldic League are still on site waiting for orders from their captains. These wanted to await the results of the negotiations between the Protestant Estates and King Ferdinand I. at the Diet in Nürnberg. It is also reported of two fugitives, one of whom escaped, while the other was captured.
Stockmeister Anton Zili acknowledges the receipt of 120 gulden by Junker Jakob Kunz. The 120 gulden were donated by Elsbeth Bruder for the poor people of the Stockamt in St. Gallen.

Kaspar Korn, hospital master at the new hospital in Nürnberg, writes to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen. He reminds them that his late father, Hans Kern the Elder, was a citizen of St. Gallen for many years. Out of necessity, his father had to move to Nürnberg with his late mother and the children (Kaspar and his now deceased siblings) and accept citizenship there. Out of gratitude towards the authorities of St. Gallen, who had still offered support to his father, as to a citizen of St. Gallen, during his move to Nürnberg and the resulting renunciation of his St. Gallen citizenship, Korn sends a gift to St. Gallen. It is a book by Martin Luther, which has recently appeared. The title is "Wider die Juden und ihre Lügen", in which the errors and the cunning of the Jews, the Pope, and the Turks are set out. He asks that this be read aloud or circulated among the council members for reading.

The council envoys of the 13 cantons of the Confederation, assembled in Baden, ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to prevent the purchase and export of gunpowder and saltpeter, as this could run counter to the interests of the Confederate cantons. The Emperor is trying to purchase gunpowder and saltpeter throughout the Confederation under the pretext of using it against the Duke of Geldern and Kleve.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, upon their request, on the proceedings of the Diet in Baden. Zürich had convened the Diet to dissuade the Confederate allies from the French wars and thus to secure peace in the common fatherland. The other cantons, however, rejected this and instead wanted to send an embassy to the Emperor together with Bern and Zürich, in order to negotiate a peace with the help of the Imperial Estates. Zürich and Bern considered this unfeasible as long as the Confederate mercenaries still openly stand in the Feld against the Emperor. The messengers also lacked the mandate to reply to a letter transmitted by the Imperial Estates, in which a complaint is raised against the Confederate support of the French King. The reply to this is to be discussed on 20 April in Baden. Zürich encloses a copy of the letter of the Imperial Estates, promises to report after the Diet, and in turn asks for the forwarding of news that come to St. Gallen for Zürich's merchants or others.

The Estates and Princes of the Empire ask the Confederate cantons to end the mercenary alliance with the French King, Franz I., and to no longer send mercenaries into his service. Landsknechts who are in the service of the French King are to be recalled. The French King has not only attacked and conquered territories of the Emperor Karl V., but has also allied himself with the Ottomans. He is therefore considered an enemy of Christendom and of the Empire. The Confederates are to keep their distance from him and to support the Empire and the Emperor.

Schultheiss and Council of Bern inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the receipt of the aid request sent to them in the name of the St. Gallen citizen and carrier Matthias Ziegler. Matthias Ziegler had linen stolen from his wagon in the Bernese territory, as he had left his wagon alone in the Feld at night to go to the nearest village, which is why he also bears some guilt. Suspects have already been interrogated, but no success has been achieved. Bern regrets the incident and promises to continue pursuing the crime and to deliver Ziegler his goods as soon as they reappear.

The Burgomaster, the small and large Council of Zürich send the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, in an enclosure, news from the camp at Carignano regarding the victory of the French and the Confederates over the Emperor.
Report from Wilhelm Fröhlich to the Burgomaster and Council of Zürich from the camp of Carignano about the victory of the French and the Confederates over the Emperor.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich apologize to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for the delayed report on a Confederate diet in Baden around the imperial defeat at Carignano. By sending a copy of the diet, they make up for the omission and report that Bern does not yet know whether it has signed the enclosed diet.

The Diet takes a position in a joint letter on the accusations of the Emperor and the Imperial Estates that they support the King of Frankreich through foreign services, who is in an alliance with the Ottomans. In this way, the Confederates endanger the whole of Christendom.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the victory of the King of Frankreich, Franz I., in the Battle of Ceresole in Piemont against the Emperor Karl V. and various developments in the Italian War. As an enclosure, a copy of a reply letter from the Imperial Estates and Imperial Cities to the 13 cantons of the Confederation regarding the Diet in Baden is sent along.

The Electors, Princes, and Estates of the Empire assembled at the Imperial Diet in Speyer confirm to the 13 cantons of the Confederation assembled in Baden the receipt of their response concerning the mercenary question. The response of the Diet, that neither Confederate captains nor mercenaries in the service of the French King had known of his alliance with the Ottomans against the Emperor, is strongly doubted.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the peace negotiations between Emperor Karl V. and the French King Franz I. In addition, a kaiserliches Mandat is reported, which obliges payments and for which they are striving with the Emperor for its revocation. In an enclosure, further news are also communicated.

Reports of various authors from the camp of Ceresole during the Fourth Italian War between Frankreich and the Empire, containing information on the Confederates' mercenaries and a copy of a letter to the Count of Oria concerning the wars against the Turks.

Referring to an earlier letter (Missive 631), the Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the conduct of the Confederate cantons in dealing with the tax demanded by the Emperor in the war against the Turks, for the settlement of which the city of St. Gallen had also been requested by Speyer to pay 1700 gulden to Augsburg. Two enclosures are sent along to provide information on the Confederates' handling of these demands.
Summary of the deliberations of the Diet regarding the further course of action of the Burgomaster and Council of Basel concerning the Turkish tax demanded by the Emperor from the city of Basel.
Report on the siege of Saint-Dizier.

Elisabeth, Abbess of the Cistercian nunnery of Magdenau, writes to the town clerk of St. Gallen regarding the transfer of the farm at Gebertschwil in Oberbüren. The monastery is the owner of the farm, which lies in the territory of the monastery of St. Gallen. The court lord is the bailiff of Oberdorf. The Abbess asks the town clerk to draft the document in her and the convent's name. She, the convent, and the abbot would then authenticate the document with their seal, but it is not strictly necessary that the Abbess seal it.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the peace negotiations regarding the County and the Duchy of Burgundy between the French King and the Emperor. An attached copy of a letter from the Lord of Blancfosse contains furthermore a report on the capture of the town of Saint-Dizier by imperial troops.

Copy of a report on a letter from the Herr von Blancfosse to the Burgomaster and Council of Zürich dated 30 August 1544, which reports on the capture of the town of Saint-Dizier by imperial troops and on the state of the French army.

Theodor Brand, Burgomaster of Basel, and the secret Council of Basel warn the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen against foreign spies, who wish to drive Frenchmen residing in the Confederation or their goods out of the Confederation. In particular, Basel, Solothurn, Schaffhausen, St. Gallen, and other Confederate cantons, which host many French persons, goods, or establishments, are affected by the practices of these spies. The Burgomaster and secret Council of Basel therefore ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to warn the Frenchmen who are staying in St. Gallen and to keep an eye on strangers.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the latest developments regarding the peace negotiations between the Duchy and the County of Burgundy. Zürich mediates on behalf of the Confederation in this regard between the plenipotentiaries of the Emperor and the French King. Burgomaster and Council of Zürich also refer to the enclosure, in which the royal advocate Blancfosse reports on new developments in the territories in Piemont disputed between the Emperor and the King, on the state of the imperial troops, and on negotiations between the conflicting parties. According to Zürich, both parties communicate differently and to their own advantage.

The Herr von Blancfosse informs about communications from the French King to the Confederates concerning the current situation of various battlefields, armies and battles as well as peace negotiations with the Emperor.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the peace settlement between the Emperor and the French King had come about, according to an enclosed copy of a letter from the Herr von Blancfosse to Zürich. In a postscript of the same date, however, Burgomaster and Council of Zürich report that, according to reports to the contrary, the peace settlement had been destroyed by an imperial attack on the French army. Since the former news is more positive and also of a more recent date, they wish to believe it. As soon as Zürich receives the peace treaty, they wish to inform St. Gallen.

The Herr von Blancfosse informs the Burgomaster and Council of Zürich about a peace that is said to have been concluded and published in Paris between the Emperor and the French King. He also conveys that the French King assured him that he did not wish to forget the Confederates and their help.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich confirm in haste to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen the peace settlement between the Emperor and the French King, already announced in an earlier letter from the Lord of Blancfosse. An envoy of the French King had personally informed them in Zürich about the peace settlement. Part of this peace is the planned marriage between the Emperor's daughter and the French King's son, the Duke of Orléans. As a dowry, the Imperial Niederlande, as well as the Duchy of Mailand and the County of Burgund, are to pass into the possession of the Duke of Orléans after the death of the Emperor. The Emperor is to give the Duke a ton of gold annually from the use of the Duchy of Mailand. The French King is to renounce the Duchy of Savoyen. Confederate troops are still in service for the French King against the King of England, to move the latter to peace.

Burgomaster and Council of Nördlingen ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to support the petition of their citizen Paul Gall, Binder, attached to the missive. In the name of his mother, a citizen of Nördlingen, Gall asks for an interrogation of the St. Gallen citizen Martin Hux. His testimony is to be recorded in a sealed document and handed over to Paul Gall. The latter will bear the costs.

Paul Gall, Binder and citizen of Nördlingen, asks the Burgomaster and Council of Nördlingen in the name of his mother for support. His mother needs a written proof that she is unjustly accused of the previous theft of a piece of linen from a citizen of St. Gallen named Martin Hux. Martin Hux himself had already interrogated the mother of Paul Gall and is convinced of her innocence. Paul Gall therefore asks the Burgomaster and Council of Nördlingen for a letter of safe conduct or passport, so that he himself may go to St. Gallen to obtain there a statement from Hux sealed by the authority of St. Gallen.

Burgomaster and Council of Isny ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to show the St. Gallen bleaching grounds to their two bleachers and their town master builder, the bearer of the letter, because the linen does not become white on the two bleaching grounds in Isny. In contrast, they have reports that the bleaching grounds in St. Gallen are very well arranged and such problems as in Isny therefore do not exist.

Ambrosius Falk again asks the Council of St. Gallen for a winter coat, consisting of a jacket and woolen trousers, so that he may all the better fulfill his civic service in winter, provided that God preserves him in good health.

Ammann and Council of Appenzell ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to send them a sworn gauger, so that their grain and other measures can be checked. For they have secretly learned that some measures used in their land are too small. They ask for the confidential disclosure of the date, so that no one makes the measures disappear before the inspection.

Niklaus Ruch asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to cover the expenses incurred by his move, in particular for tolls in Diessenhofen, Stein, Steckborn and Konstanz. He says that he had forgotten to report this, but that it is customary in the Confederation for officials to receive such support.

Clemens Hör, teacher at the city's German school in St. Gallen, complains to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the competition of a certain Jörg Walch, who also teaches the young people elementary knowledge in arithmetic and writing for payment. This poses a problem for Clemens Hör, as he thereby loses earning opportunities.

Clemens Hör, teacher at the city's German school in St. Gallen, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to have his school publicly announced again in the church by a preacher or town servant on the coming Sunday. The Council had previously ordered him to interrupt the instruction for fourteen days, whereupon a rumor about a contagious disease in his household spread among the population. Hör clarifies that his sick son has fully recovered. He also renews his request for financial support, which he has already made several times, as the two florins of the churchwarden are not sufficient to maintain his household without students.

Clemens Hör, teacher at the city's German school in St. Gallen, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to allow him to teach more children. He complains about the growing competitive pressure. Contrary to the city ordinance, which allows a maximum of ten pupils per teacher, a certain Jörg Walch has disregarded this. As a result, hardly enough pupils remain for the petitioner Clemens Hör for him to be able to earn his livelihood. Furthermore, he asks the authorities to enforce the ordinance established years ago, which states that a schoolmaster is not obliged to accept pupils who do not already master the basics of reading and writing German.

The Schultheiss and Council of Winterthur inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about a band of robbers which has killed 21 persons. The band of robbers consists of Jakob von Rapperswil, Klaus von Strassburg, the tanner Joop von Strassburg, who has a boy with him, Bernhard and Niklaus von Strassburg, brothers of the bodyguard, Valentin Wyss, Niklaus Scherer and Jakob Dietrich, all from Strassburg. In addition, two other persons from Porrentruy, about whom nothing further is known, were also present. Besides these murderers and thieves, a Hans Schwyzer from Solothurn is also mentioned, who is also a murderer and thief, but who was not present.

Emperor Karl V. informs the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he has convened an Imperial Diet in Regensburg, at which he will participate in person. At the same time, Karl again emphasizes his good will towards the Confederation. The St. Gallen are to give no credence to any contrary rumors. They received further information through the bearer of this letter.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the Lords of the County of Burgundy have had the inheritance settlement money sent to them by their Chamberlain of the Confederation. The men of Zürich ask the men of St. Gallen whether they should deliver their part against a receipt or whether they should hand over the money at the annual accounts in Baden. In addition, they send them a letter that is to be delivered to them at the request of the Imperial Majesty.

Lux Ritter, former Captain of St. Gallen, asks Ambrosius Eigen, Säckelmeister in St. Gallen, to use his influence with the St. Gallen authorities for the foundation of a coat-of-arms window at the open inn Zum Roten Turm in Luzern, as the other Confederate cantons would also do.
Burgomaster and Council of Zürich request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to observe and inform, via the messenger, about war preparations in Bregenz.

Hans Blum and Othmar Fridbolt, who had entered into mercenary service despite a prohibition and were therefore expelled from the city with their families, ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to allow them to explain and answer for themselves before the Council.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich thank Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for the received letter and the accompanying information, coupled with the request to continue to be informed about incidents and events. They would do the same in turn.

Schultheiss and Council of Bern thank Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for the letters sent to their Secret Council. The Bernese inform that a Diet is to be held in Baden to deliberate on what might be of the greatest benefit to the Confederates and the neighbors of Konstanz. The arrival is set for Sunday evening, 27. February, at the inn. The Bernese ask the St. Gallen to inform Zürich, Glarus, Schaffhausen and Appenzell just as they have, and to write to Luzern and the four cantons Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden and Zug as well as Freiburg and Solothurn.

Burgomaster and Council of Lindau report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen on a witness examination in the context of a legal dispute pending before the Council of St. Gallen between the brothers Joachim and Galle Mayer of Herisau on the one hand and the citizen of St. Gallen Erasmus Schuhmacher, called Gügge, on the other hand. On the basis of a judgment letter issued by St. Gallen, five witnesses, Endres Pfefferlin, Jakob Oberreuter, Anna Schlappritzi, Elsa Scheibinger and Margaretha Rainher, were individually and under oath questioned. Their statements are attached. Lindau also informs that Erasmus Schuhmacher has broken his oath made to the Council of Lindau not to leave the city without permission.

A report sent by the Burgomaster and Council of Lindau to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen concerning the witness depositions of Endres Pfefferlin, Jakob Oberreuter, Anna Schlappritzi, Elsa Scheibinger and Margaretha Rainher regarding a violent quarrel.

Jakob Hafner, cellar master in the monastery at Pfäfers, asks Dr. Joachim von Watt, Burgomaster of St. Gallen, to intervene so that he does not lose his citizenship. He says that he accepted foreign services solely out of the necessity to earn his livelihood. Furthermore, his siblings, who own the house in St. Gallen, pay taxes and watch money like other citizens of St. Gallen. He is also willing to do so, provided he returns to reside there, which Captain Jörg Schenk, the bearer of this letter, can explain.

Johannes Haab, former Burgomaster of Zürich, and Italhans Domeisen inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen from Baden that neither the abbot of St. Gallen nor the Appenzeller messenger had mentioned anything that concerned the citizens of St. Gallen. They further thank them for the written information, which they will forward to their superiors. Finally, they inform them about the events in Frankreich and in Deutschland, in particular about the Schmalkaldic War, and about the fact that the French king assumes that the necessary mercenaries will not be denied to him. For this purpose, the 11 cantons have appointed a negotiation in Solothurn after Easter, in order to answer the king afterwards.

Burgomaster and Council of Isny ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to ensure that in the inheritance matter of Wolf Zollikofer's widow, the company in which Zollikofer was involved, may finally have an examination of the company's registers and accounts carried out. Since the company has so far refused, it is not possible to determine who is entitled to how much, and the dispute cannot be settled. The correspondence between Isny and Jakob Zollikofer is attached.

Burgomaster and Council of Isny request, on behalf of the widow and the children of the deceased Wolf Zollikofer and their supporters Jörg Ballauf and Kaspar Bufler, the partner Jakob Zollikofer to re-examine the division of the inheritance based on the registers and accounts in St. Gallen. The amount of the intended inheritance seems to them to be too low. The examination could finally put an end to the dispute and help the survivors. They request a written communication with the messenger.

Jakob Zollikofer, partner, answers the Burgomaster and Council of Isny in the inheritance matter of the widow of Wolf Zollikofer. Wolf Zollikofer had taken out and consumed more from the partnership than he had put in. What he had used the money for is uncertain. However, they owe each other nothing, which had already been communicated to the guardians of the widow earlier.

Burgomaster and Council of Isny inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen in the inheritance matter of Wolf Zollikofer that the assistants of the widow Zollikofer, the town Ammann Jörg Ballauf and Kaspar Bufler, together with Kaspar Eberz, citizen of Isny, have made themselves ready to come to St. Gallen for the announced and desired inspection of the account books of the partnership of Jakob Zollikofer. They ask the St. Gallen authorities again for support.

Schultheiss and Council of Frauenfeld ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for support. Hans Spul, their citizen, complained about his son-in-law Melchior Grübel, a citizen of St. Gallen, who leads a dissolute life, behaves improperly, treats his daughter badly, and is deceiving her with a foreign woman. The people of Frauenfeld ask the people of St. Gallen to interrogate Melchior Grübel and put him in his place, so that the woman, who has never caused any unpleasantness in Frauenfeld, does not also lose her property through her husband.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to appear on the evening of 20 November in Baden at the inn. At a Confederate Diet on the following day, Monday 21 November, the incidents in Bellinzona and in other Common Lordships, as well as the dangers associated with them, are to be discussed.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich thank Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for the information sent. Since a Diet has been convened in Baden regarding the events and impending dangers in Bellinzona, which had been communicated to the St. Gallen in a recent letter, they considered it right to keep the information with themselves and not pass it on to the other Confederate cantons. Instead, it is to be reported in writing or orally through the St. Gallen envoys at the upcoming Diet. The Zürich ask the St. Gallen to keep them informed of any further occurrences.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich assure Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they will intercede with the King of Frankreich on behalf of a citizen of St. Gallen who is in custody in Lyon on account of his faith. At the same time, Zürich requests that the medical costs of the St. Gallen tailor Paul Renftler, who was admitted to their smallpox house and is being cared for there, be assumed.

Burgomaster and Council of Wangen ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for legal support for the widow and the children of their citizen Hans Wachter. Wachter came to his death through a killing by the son of the St. Gallen executioner Meister Bernhard Ewelacker. Bernhard Ewelacker had thereby contractually committed himself in a settlement to pay the widow and her minor children 30 gulden in four installments; three gulden immediately and subsequently nine gulden annually in the coming years. The widow has received the three gulden, but the nine gulden are still outstanding. Since the widow and the children of the slain are in great distress, Burgomaster and Council of Wangen ask that the St. Gallen authority helps to ensure that their citizen fulfills the contractual obligation.

Burgomaster and Council of Isny reply to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to their letter of inquiry, whether it is known to them that one person was executed by the wheel in a village named Weisseneck. This condemned man had confessed that he had received one hundred gulden together with others from a nobleman so that they would set a fire in St. Gallen. Isny replies that a village or hamlet named Weisseneck is unknown to them, and it is also not known to them that someone was executed by the wheel. Should they learn more about this incident, they would, however, report immediately.

Burgomaster and Council of Lindau reply to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen on their letter of information concerning arsonists. They are aware that in Stockach someone had been executed who had confessed to setting fires in villages and towns for money. It is said to have burned in Kattenhorn as well. Should they learn more, they would report again.

Michael von Landenberg, bailiff in Güttingen, reports to his cousins, brothers-in-law, and friends about war mercenaries who are settled in the County of Thurgau and who have attempted to join the Schmalkaldic League. In doing so, they have defied a prohibition of the Confederation and are to pay a fine. Landenberg demands the sending of the fine and asks for a written notification of who will send how much. He also asks for a written notification with this messenger.

Burgomaster and Council of Überlingen ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to supply them with butter due to a shortage. The butter is to be transported via Steinach by the ship that carries grain from the Überlingen weekly market to Steinach and returns. Should the butter shortage no longer exist, they would inform the St. Gallen authorities.

Burgomaster and Council of Radolfzell answer Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen regarding a letter concerning the St. Gallen grain merchants who visit their weekly market. The Radolfzell authorities state that they cannot recall that the matter connected with the Emperor and Konstanz has anything to do with them or the St. Gallen people. The Radolfzell authorities will hold the weekly market on Tuesdays beginning on 14 August and as before the time of the uprising. The St. Gallen people are invited to visit the market without restriction on the number and as before the uprising. There is also no warlike troop present anymore.

The six Confederate cantons Zürich, Bern, Luzern, Schwyz, Zug and Glarus answer the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to a letter in which the citizens of St. Gallen complain that they had not been informed, like the other Confederate cantons and the abbot of the monastery of St. Gallen, that they should arm themselves due to the insecure situation. Nevertheless, the citizens of St. Gallen had sent a company to provide support. The senders apologize for the omission, asserting that this had not happened intentionally, but due to a misunderstanding in the communication. Furthermore, they assure the city of St. Gallen of their support in this difficult time.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich answer Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen regarding a letter in which the citizens of St. Gallen complain that they had not been informed about the uncertain situation like the other Confederate cantons. The citizens of Zürich reaffirm that this had not been done intentionally. The information given to the abbot of the monastery of St. Gallen had been provided at his request, because he had inquired how he should conduct himself. Furthermore, they have no new information, except that the Confederates at Rottweil informed the Diet at Baden that the Imperial ban and supreme ban had been pronounced against Konstanz.

Burgomaster and Council of Überlingen ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to retain the estate of the wife of Diethelm Payer, who died in Konstanz, until the situation in Konstanz improves and the succession to the heirs, one of whom is a granddaughter under lawful guardianship in Überlingen, can take place in due order. They also ask that the estate be inventoried and a copy of the inventory be sent to the guardians of the children.

Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that it is known to them that several of their citizens from their suburb Petershausen, who had been damaged, as well as other people who falsely claim to be damaged citizens of Konstanz, were seeking help and alms. However, at present, the supply in Konstanz is secured, which is why they warn the St. Gallen authorities against such fraudulent people.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for written information with this messenger in the case of the tailor Balthasar Ringler, who is sitting in their prison and is being subjected to the torture. According to his wife Margaretha Fryg of Stammheim, who has denounced him for simultaneous marriage promises to three women and robbery, Ringler comes from the city of St. Gallen, where he previously lived with his first wife, Anna Högger of Ilanz, from whom he was divorced. However, she ran away when Ringler, due to lack of money, forced her into prostitution with the monks in the monastery. For this reason, Ringler was taken into custody in St. Gallen, but subsequently released again. Ringler confessed under torture, but since the Zürich authorities do not believe Ringler's statements, they ask for information about his person.

The ten cantons of the Confederation assembled in Baden ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that their former Burgomaster Joachim von Watt mediate as chairman in the dispute concerning the punishment of the mercenaries of the Landgrafschaft Thurgau between the seven cantons Zürich, Luzern, Uri, Schwyz, Unterwalden, Zug and Glarus on the one hand and the three cantons Bern, Freiburg and Solothurn on the other hand. In the event of an acceptance, they would deliver all the legal documents. They ask for a written answer with this messenger.

Burgomaster and administrator of the captaincy of Konstanz Hans Muntprat responds to a request for legal assistance from Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen. The entrepreneur Alexander Payer asserts that he was promised a dowry of 600 to 1000 gulden through his marriage to a daughter of Schlappritzis. Upon the request of Payer's lawyer Hans Syber of Schaffhausen, this is now confirmed after the interrogation of a witness at the wedding.
Hieronymus Sailer asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to allow him to remain in their citizenship. This is particularly important as security for his financial transactions in Frankreich.
Hieronymus Sailer again asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to confirm his citizenship of St. Gallen.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen complain to Georg Speth von Sulzburg, Imperial Councillor and Captain of Konstanz, as well as Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz, about the unlawful conduct of the brothers Felix and Jakob Grimmel against the St. Gallen creditors of Hans Ulrich Rüegger, citizen of St. Gallen. The St. Gallen authorities request a written reply.

Georg Tschudi, Abbot of the collegiate foundation at Kreuzlingen, also on behalf of Konstanz, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to intervene in the conflict with the brothers Felix and Jakob Grimmel regarding the confiscation of linen and the threat of auction. It would be best if their citizens would calm down and could decide in favor of an amicable solution.

Burgomaster and Council of Nürnberg write to Statthalter and Council of St. Gallen, saying that they regret and condemn the attack on merchants of St. Gallen. The citizens of Nürnberg assure the citizens of St. Gallen that they will work for the pursuit of the robbers, but point out that the deed took place on the sovereign territory of Margrave Georg Friedrich I. von Brandenburg-Ansbach, whereby he is responsible for security. Furthermore, they mention that it would have been well if the victims had handled their goods more cautiously and been more discreet, for then they could not have been so easily scouted.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich request, in the name of the St. Gallen woman Magdalena Horber, Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to use their influence to secure financial support for Magdalena from her relatives in St. Gallen. Magdalena Horber was bitten by a snake while working in Unterwalden. Previous treatments were unsuccessful; she can now have herself cured by a Zürich bather and needs money to pay his wages.

Statthalter and Council of Appenzell write to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen and inform them about the unauthorized sale of wood by their resident (Hintersasse), the son of Hans Knecht from Teufen.

Schultheiss and Council of Winterthur ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to take in and care for Magdalena Horber, the daughter of the deceased citizen of St. Gallen Hans Horber, who is lying in their hospital. Magdalena Horber was bitten by a snake during the hay harvest and subsequently had to have her leg amputated. Her distress now demands that a Christian authority take her in.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the latest events regarding the planned Confederation peace mission in Frankreich. In addition to the four Evangelical towns, the five Catholic cantons of the Innerschweiz as well as Glarus and the Drei Bünde in Churwalden have now decided to participate. The request to the French ambassador in Solothurn, where the King of Frankreich is currently staying and where he intends to meet the Confederation delegation, is still open. Zürich again asks the St. Gallen to also participate with an envoy, asks for a response, and indicates that it will announce the assembly point of the delegation as soon as it is determined.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich invite Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to a Confederate Diet in Baden on 12 December. Concerned about the religious war in Frankreich, Zürich wishes to send a peace mission to the neighbouring country together with Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen and to negotiate with the French King. The organisation and the instructions of this embassy are to be discussed at the Diet.

Ammann and Council of Appenzell write to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen and inform them that the night watchmen had observed a firelight on the previous Tuesday at midnight. The fire watchmen were immediately woken so that they could inquire where the fire was located and how help could be provided. The fire affected Appenzell farmers. The Appenzell people thank the people of St. Gallen for the spontaneously offered help.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich write to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they are well informed, through their envoys who participated in the last Confederate Diet at Baden, about the negotiations with Frankreich. A further Diet has been agreed for 6 March. The peace mission to Frankreich and the meeting with the French ambassador in Solothurn are to be discussed. Zürich offers St. Gallen to represent their concerns, whereby St. Gallen as well as other allied cantons could save expenses.

Ammann and Council of Appenzell inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have received their letter, in which the citizens of St. Gallen complain about the sale of Luggmilch on Friday by Appenzellers. The Appenzellers will now have the prohibition read out in a mandate in the churches located near the St. Gallen market on the following Sunday. In addition, the Appenzellers ask the citizens of St. Gallen to ensure that the acceptance of the French pfennigs in St. Gallen is not refused.

Ammann and Council of Appenzell ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to continue accepting the Dick Pfennig at 23 kreuzer until an agreement is reached. They ask for a written reply with this messenger.

Ammann and Council of Appenzell repeatedly call on Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to settle the coin dispute. In doing so, they mention that the Appenzell countrymen of St. Gallen had already previously been plagued by the yarn trade. Furthermore, the accusation of the pre-purchase of Luggmilch is ridiculous and mocking. They ask for a written reply with this messenger.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen reply to a letter from the Landammann and Council of Appenzell, in which the latter had complained about incitement and seditious speeches by citizens of St. Gallen and newly admitted citizens against the ecclesiastical and secular authority of Appenzell, as well as about incitement to shedding blood. The St. Gallen authorities assure them that they will not let such offenses go unpunished, provided they can be proven, but refer to the fact that Appenzellers had also engaged in improper speech in the city of St. Gallen. Regarding the newly admitted citizens, they state that they have not admitted any new citizens for a long time, and affirm that the former Appenzell residents tolerated among them were behaving quietly and reservedly.

Landammann and Council of Appenzell again complain to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the overbearing behavior of citizens of St. Gallen and newly admitted citizens towards the countrymen of Appenzell. These are being incited by the St. Gallen citizens against the spiritual and secular authority of Appenzell, instigated to disobedience, and even led to shedding blood. Appenzell expressly objects to citizens of St. Gallen preachers or secular persons interfering in its government. The Appenzell people call on the St. Gallen people to grant free access to the market and in the future to work for peace, quiet, and unity for the good of the fatherland. If this is not complied with, they reserve the right to seek other counsel.

The Landammann and Council of Appenzell ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to inform their countrymen who have moved away because of their faith and have become new citizens in St. Gallen that they are no longer to participate in the Appenzell Landsgemeinde.

Landammann and Council of Appenzell inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the shameful, vicious speeches of Melchior Glinz and Paul Jakob, citizens of St. Gallen, in Urnäsch, and ask the St. Gallen authorities to act in this matter before they themselves will take action against it.

Landammann and Council of Appenzell complain to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about incitement against them and conflicts over the yarn trade and other matters. They say that they had already pointed this out to the St. Gallen authorities several times, both orally and in writing, but the St. Gallen authorities had not reacted accordingly, which is why they now turned to the 12 cantons of the Confederation allied with Appenzell. Attached is a copy of a report on the ill words of the St. Gallen citizen Kaspar Brisig in Gais.
Report of the malicious speech and incitement of the St. Gallen citizen Kaspar Brisig in Gais against the authorities and the country people of Appenzell.

The Schultheiss, Landammann and Councils of the five Catholic cantons in Luzern ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen not to interfere in the disturbances around Jost Jakob in the Land of Appenzell. They ask for a written answer with the messenger.

Landammann Johannes Tanner and Council of Appenzell ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to ensure that in future no more citizens of St. Gallen participate in the Appenzell Landsgemeinde. For many people from the neighbourhood had stood in the Landsgemeinde and had taken part in the election of officials, and not only by raising one hand, but two. The citizens of St. Gallen are to ensure that on the day of the Landsgemeinde their own people stay with them, just as they ensured that on the election day of the Council of St. Gallen their countrymen stayed with them.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen intercede with Joachim Volkmar, Colonel and General Major of the Swedish Army and Commandant of Überlingen, on behalf of two of their citizens. These had bought small barrels of salt, which were to be sent to them on a ship of Lindau. This ship had been intercepted by soldiers under Volkmar's command and the cargo had been taken to Überlingen. Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request the Commandant that the small barrels of salt be released and returned to the buyers free of charge and without delay.

Joachim von Volkmar, Colonel and Lieutenant General of the Swedish Army, responds to a petition from the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen. It concerns small barrels of salt that had been taken from citizens of St. Gallen on a ship of Lindau. Volkmar recalls that he had recently, in a similar case, returned goods that belonged to citizens of St. Gallen but had been on enemy ships. He is still ready to render all friendly services to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen and to the whole Confederation. However, if citizens of St. Gallen, despite warning, allowed their goods to be transported on enemy ships, which contravened the prohibition of the Generality, the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen could not expect that he would give such goods back, especially since everyone knew that he was only allowed to use Confederate ships.

Burgomaster and Council of Kaufbeuren request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for a loan of at least 4'000 gulden for the payment of the Swedish satisfaction payments. Kaufbeuren has received the order to bring a total of 6'200 gulden to Ulm within a month's deadline. However, this is impossible for the citizenry after the years of war turmoil. To secure the loan claim, Kaufbeuren would pledge the villages of Westendorf and Dösingen to the city of St. Gallen. The loan would be interest-bearing and repaid after four years.

Martin Mathias Rader, as envoy of Kaufbeuren, requests a loan of at least 1500 to 2000 gulden from the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen. The money is to be used to finally move the Swedish garrison troops to withdraw. It is not possible for the citizenry to raise the amount itself. The entire citizenry will be liable for the debt and it will be repaid in six years with annual interest. It is known how the Papists had tried for 40 years to exterminate and root out the Gospel. The Thirty Years' War then arose from this. In 1628, the Papists had removed the preachers and the schoolmasters from the city of Kaufbeuren, introduced the Jesuits, and taken away the property and goods of the Evangelicals. Thanks to the peace settlement of 1648, the Papists had to withdraw again, the Jesuits were expelled again, the city government and all Ämter were handed back to the Evangelicals, and the property and goods were returned to those who had been driven out.
Kaufbeuren requests Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for a loan. The money is to be used to pay Swedish claims for satisfaction, which amount to a total of 12400 gulden.

Bartholomäus Anhorn, Stadtpfarrer in St. Gallen, has received leave from the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen and reports to the Council on the course of events. Upon arriving in Heidelberg, he says that he was asked to preach in various churches, including in Mosbach, and to cleanse the churches of Catholicism. The Elector of the Palatinate personally attended his sermon and asked him to take possession of the 24 parishes in the Mosbach inspection, to remove the Jesuits, monks, and pastors, and to remove the idols in the churches and to preach. Anhorn hopes for the understanding of the Burgomaster and Council regarding his longer absence. He says that upon his return he will settle the debts of himself and his brother-in-law and will hold several sermons for this purpose. The creditors wanted to sell his estate Bernegg below its value to cover his debts. He asks the Burgomaster and Council for support and assures them of later payment of his debts. Furthermore, Anhorn reports that the Evangelical cities and cantons intended to send a delegation to the Elector of the Palatinate to congratulate him on the retaking of the land. In addition, Anhorn reports on the dire situation west of the Rhine, for the alleviation of which the Evangelical churches of the Confederation would be approached one last time for support. In contrast, Heidelberg, located east of the Rhine, is doing better; it is hoped that Heidelberg will have fully recovered in two years.

Barthlomäus Anhorn, citizen of St. Gallen and pastor in Mosbach, reports to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that he has already requested several times to come closer to his homeland again, but has not yet been able to obtain a release. Rather, he has been asked not to leave the church in the lurch in these times of distress, which he does not intend to do. He hopes that the Burgomaster and Council will not take this amiss. He was called to be pastor and inspector in Mosbach. However, this call seems to be being revoked, especially since in the fourth week in Heidelberg he was asked by the elector's councillors, by the citizenry, and even by the Lutherans to remain in Heidelberg. The citizenry promised him, in addition to the regular living, a considerable additional compensation. In the meantime, however, he adheres to the call to Mosbach.

Wolfgang Meyer, cathedral preacher in Basel, hands over to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen a booklet written by him, in which he so clearly displays the power and authority of the Christian authorities that no one can have any doubts anymore. Therefore, the theological faculty has decided on the translation into the Latin language, so that the booklet would become accessible to all nations. Wolfgang Meyer asks the Burgomaster and Council for forgiveness for having troubled them with his request.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that they have contributed 12 gulden to Doctor Wolfgang Meyer, cathedral preacher in Basel, for his gifted booklet. Their envoy and those of three other benefitted evangelical cities had recommended at the Diet in Baden that each canton contribute ten gulden or Kronen.

Burgomaster and Council of Chur ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for mediation in a conflict over a marriage contract between Emerita Cleric of Chur and her relatives on the one hand and Georg Spindler, citizen of St. Gallen, former Säckelmeister, on the other hand. Since Georg Spindler is in financial difficulties with his Handelsgesellschaft and had reported to his wife's relatives in Chur that, under the given circumstances, he could no longer uphold the marriage contract concluded at the wedding and that he is already of advanced age, the female relatives fear the loss of the dowry. For the financial security of the wife and the children, Johann Tscharner, Burgomaster of Chur, and Martin Cleric, Stadtrichter of Chur, ask for help on behalf of their relative Emerita Cleric, among other things for the appointment of a guardian for the wife and the children.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request a court day in Konstanz on behalf of Hans Christoph Buff, butcher's apprentice from Gammertingen. Buff had been accused of disloyalty towards his former master, Sebastian Tobler, butcher and citizen of St. Gallen, by Leonhard Rittel from the Markgräflerland, in the presence of a member of the Council of Konstanz, Heinrich Hüetli. In order to restore his honor, Buff wishes to state his case before the Council in Konstanz and asks Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for certified statements regarding his good conduct with his former master Sebastian Tobler and his current master Ulrich Alther, guild master and citizen of St. Gallen.

The citizen of St. Gallen Christoph Tobias Studer asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to deliver his counter-report, drafted in this supplication, in the conflict over a debt claim with Magdalena, the widow of Tobias Schnitzer, citizen of Kempten, to the Burgomaster and Council of Kempten.

Burgomaster and Council of Ulm request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for a renewed loan to pay the Swedish satisfaction money. For the high billeting and provisioning costs of the militias, most of the available money has already been used up. In a postscript, the Ulm citizens offer goods to the St. Gallen citizens for sale.

Burgomaster and Council of Ulm offer in a postscript to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen as well as to the citizenry of the city of St. Gallen and their merchants powder, metal, and lead for sale against cash payment. The price can be negotiated. However, the Ulm parties assure that they can make a satisfactory offer if needed.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about a loan request submitted by Elector and Count Palatine Karl Ludwig of Heidelberg to the Evangelical cantons of the Confederation, a copy of which was attached to the letter. Zürich is well disposed towards the request but asks St. Gallen for a statement. They wish to know whether St. Gallen would in principle provide support and whether the money should be sent as a loan or as a wedding gift from the Elector to Charlotte, Landgravine of Hessen-Kassel. Zürich asks for a written answer, as the Elector's negotiator, Karl Mieg, would have requested it as well. The money could be dispatched for the beginning of the Frankfurt Easter Fair.

Karl Ludwig, Pfalzgraf bei Rhein, Erztruchsess und Kurfürst, Herzog in Bayern, informs the Evangelical cantons of the Confederation that he will soon marry Princess Charlotte von Hessen-Kassel. He would have liked to invite the addressees of the letter to the wedding festivities. Because of the difficult situation as a result of the war, he has decided not to hold any festivities. This also applies to the subjects, since everything has been devastated and they are being plagued by the foreign garrison. Karl Ludwig therefore asks for understanding and at the same time for a loan of five to six thousand Reichstaler.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request, by means of the present letter of recommendation, the Obrist, Stadthauptmann, Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz to support the butcher's servant Hans Christoph Buff of Gammertingen from the Schwäbische Alb, who is currently working for the St. Gallen citizen, butcher and guild master Ulrich Alther, in his intended lawsuit against Heinrich Hüetli of Konstanz for defamation. At Buff's request, two of his employers in St. Gallen testified before the St. Gallen authority regarding Buff's conduct to date and his good reputation.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen write to Burgomaster and Council of Chur regarding the inquiry from Chur concerning the assets of the property brought into the marriage by the wife of Georg Spindler. At the request of the Chur authorities, Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen questioned Georg Spindler about his financial circumstances. He stated that he could not currently release the wife's property because his trading firm was in a difficult situation. He hopes for better business in the future. Two assistants from the St. Gallen Council are appointed to the wife, who will represent her interests in the future.

Countess Johannette zu Erbach asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for a loan of 1000 gulden. She says that due to the war her subjects have been murdered or have become completely impoverished, which is why she herself no longer has any income from rents and interest. She asks for a loan so that she, as a widow, can provide for her livelihood, and promises eternal gratitude as well as the repayment of the loan.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen answer Burgomaster and Council of Ulm on their request for a further loan to pay the Swedish satisfaction money. St. Gallen declines the request, pointing out that the city, due to many bankruptcies and the standstill of trade, no longer has any reserves either. Furthermore, a fire recently broke out in the suburb, through which several houses burned down. 13 households are therefore in the greatest distress, and the city has the duty to provide support.

Schultheiss and Council of Winterthur ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to admit the daughter of their citizen and church servant Heinrich Krütli to the citizenship of St. Gallen. The occasion is the engagement of Krütli's daughter to the tailor Cornelius Cunz, a citizen of St. Gallen. To be admitted to the citizenship of St. Gallen, the woman requires, according to the town law, a fortune of 200 gulden, which the father, however, cannot give her. Schultheiss and Council of Winterthur therefore ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for an exception.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen with a copy of a reply letter from Archduke Ferdinand Karl von Österreich-Tirol in Innsbruck regarding a complaint by the Confederate cantons about tariff increases in the Austrian lands. Since the Archduke demands further information on the Confederate claim in addition to what has already been received, Burgomaster and Council of Zürich ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to obtain information from the merchants of St. Gallen, as they would conduct the most trade with Austria. The statements of the merchants of St. Gallen are to be sent in writing to Zürich.

Ferdinand Karl, Archduke of Österreich-Tirol, responds to a complaint submitted to him on 20 December 1649 by the 13 cantons of the Confederation, which they discussed at the Diet of Baden on the same date. The Confederates therein requested the repeal of the tariff increases following the conclusion of the Peace of Westphalia and the observance of the hereditary agreement existing between Habsburg and the Confederation. Ferdinand Karl rejects the request with the remark that the tariffs for the merchants of the Confederation had never been increased. He is to be provided with more precise information regarding the goods allegedly subjected to higher tariffs as well as the tariff stations, so that he could make a decision on this basis.

Burgomaster and Council of Schaffhausen ask the Burgomaster, the small and large Council of St. Gallen for a legal decision in an inheritance matter of the family Zollikofer in favor of their citizen Hieronymus Peyer, who had appealed to the authorities of Schaffhausen in the name of his mother, Elisabeth Peyer-Zollikofer. The conflict over the distribution of the inheritance of Bartholome Zollikofer, Stadthauptmann and citizen of St. Gallen, who died 11 months ago, is decided based on an appeal to the small and large Council of St. Gallen.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen reply to Countess Johannette zu Erbach regarding her request for a loan of 1000 gulden. St. Gallen cannot give her the money due to its own poor financial situation.

The Landammann, captains, and Council of the Kirchhöri Herisau express their condolences to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen over the fire in the St. Gallen suburb, in which nine to ten houses burned down. Since rumors are circulating that the Herisau people knew of the fire in St. Gallen but had not sent any help, they assure them that although they had seen the fire, they could not locate it and believed it to be far away. Had they known that the fire was in St. Gallen, they would have sent their help.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen transmit to Schultheiss and Council of Frauenfeld, with their letter of recommendation, a petition from those citizens of St. Gallen who, as directors, administer the assets taken over from the company of Hans Fitler Gebrüder and co-relatives. These directors have a debt claim against Franziskus Hurter, citizen of Frauenfeld. Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request, in their accompanying letter, that the attorney of the directors be admitted before the courts of Frauenfeld.

The enclosure concerns the creditors of the Fitler inheritance. The Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen transmit to the Schultheiss and Council of Frauenfeld, with their letter of recommendation, a supplication from those citizens of St. Gallen who, as directors, administer the assets taken over from the company of Hans Fitler Gebrüder und Mitverwandten. These directors have a debt claim against Franziskus Hurter, a citizen of Frauenfeld. The Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request, in their accompanying letter, that the attorney of the directors be admitted before the courts of Frauenfeld.

Ulrich Trüeb, Ammann of Arbon, asks Sebastian Schobinger, Burgomaster of St. Gallen, not to punish those citizens of St. Gallen who were invited to the wedding of Franziskus Meder, citizen of Arbon, and who took part in a dance in the house of the bridegroom and are therefore summoned before the authority of St. Gallen. The honor dance at the wedding had been officially approved, which is why a punishment should be waived.

The administrator of the captaincy, the Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz, in the name of their hospital, ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to persuade their citizen Melchior Schobinger to agree to an extension of one to two years for the repayment of a credit that Schobinger has lent to the hospital of Konstanz. The causes are the poor economic and financial situation of the hospital of Konstanz due to crop failures of grain and wine, hospital properties on the north bank of Lake Constance destroyed by the war, the war installations burdening them, and the increasing impoverishment of the citizenry of Konstanz.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about a loan to Karl Ludwig, Pfalzgraf of Heidelberg, which he wishes to obtain from the Evangelical cantons of the Confederation. The cities of St. Gallen, Zürich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen jointly and independently of the other Confederate cantons provide a credit of 6000 Reichs thaler, of which St. Gallen is to take on a share of 1000. The money is to be handed over at the next Fronfastenmesse in Frankfurt, which is why Zürich inquires how St. Gallen intends to transmit the money. One possibility would be a joint handover, whereby the heirs of the deceased citizen of Zürich Heinrich Werdmüller could transport the money from St. Gallen to Zürich.

Johann Wilhelm, Count zu Königsegg, asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for a further loan so that he can pay his last share of the Swedish satisfaction money resulting from the Peace of Westphalia. His cousin, Count Hugo von Königsegg zu Immenstadt, stands as guarantor together with him for the repayment of the loan and the settlement of the interest. As messengers, Sebastian Bosch from Hoßkirch, staff holder and court Ammann zu Königsegg, and Martin Hornstein from the court of Königsegg, were sent. They are to give a further oral report on the necessity of a new loan and to settle the interest from last year's loan of the city of St. Gallen of 600 gulden.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen confirm to Johann Wilhelm, Count zu Königsegg und Rothenfels, the receipt of his letter and the hearing of further oral information by the envoy of the Count concerning the request for a credit to pay the Swedish satisfaction money. The request is rejected by the St. Gallen with the reference to their own precarious financial situation. The difficult situation of St. Gallen is said to be due to bankruptcies, the decline of trade, many extraordinary expenditures of the city budget, and a recent fire in the suburb. Furthermore, many other identical loan requests from friendly cities and estates, which were also rejected, have already been received, which St. Gallen also had to decline.

Ammann and Council of Appenzell Ausserrhoden ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to have their countryman Konrad Walser examined together with the St. Gallen Christian Huber, so that he may take up his position as priest in Teufen. After Konrad Walser had completed his ecclesiastical studies in Zürich and subsequently practised theology and languages in St. Gallen, he is now ready for the examination.

Schultheiss and Council of Frauenfeld answer Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen regarding their letter and the enclosed petition concerning the debt claim of the St. Gallen citizen Hans Fitler and co-relatives against the Frauenfeld citizen Franziskus Hurter. The father of Franziskus Hurter, former Schultheiss Werner Hurter, offered the St. Gallen creditors a guarantee and staggered payment of his son's debts. He had communicated his offer in writing to Jakob Fehr, substitute in St. Gallen, but has not yet received an answer. Schultheiss and Council of Frauenfeld recommend accepting the offer of Werner Hurter, as, due to inflation, the entire sum of interest and principal cannot be raised, and the creditors would then have to be satisfied with payment by movable property, goods, and wine, which might not suit them. If no agreement is reached, the debt would have to be enforced through a legal process in Frauenfeld according to the local city law.

Count Hugo von Königsegg obligates himself to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen as guarantor for a loan that his cousin Johann Wilhelm, Count zu Königsegg und Rothenfels, Lord zu Aulendorf, wishes to take out with the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to pay off the Swedish satisfaction monies.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen confirm to the Captaincy, Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz the receipt of their reply concerning a loan of 3000 gulden granted in the year 1633. Although the St. Gallen treasurer Georg Zwicker had called in the credit and demanded both the principal and the outstanding interest, and the city of St. Gallen, caused by extraordinary expenditures, is in a financially strained situation, Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen extend the repayment deadline of the loan by one to two years. They ask the Konstanzer, however, to settle the outstanding interest immediately.

The Stewards, the Captaincy, the Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for the extension of the repayment deadline of the loan of 3000 gulden, which the citizens of Konstanz had taken from the citizens of St. Gallen in 1633. The occasion for the request for extension is the demand for the return of the capital by the St. Gallen Chamberlain and Councilor Georg Zwicker.

Burgomaster and Council of Leutkirch ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for a postponement of the interest payments due since Easter in the amount of 15 gulden on a capital of 300 gulden, which St. Gallen had lent to Leutkirch in the year 1649 to settle the Swedish satisfaction payments.

Count Hugo von Königsegg asks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to continue keeping his silverware, deposited as a pledge in the hospital in St. Gallen, even though two to three interests already accrue on it. He says that he actually already had the money to redeem the pledge. However, due to Swedish satisfaction payments and the quartering of soldiers, he says that he has used up the money he had already gathered. He assures that he will settle at least the interest by Christmas at the latest and, as a reward for the accommodation, in particular to promote the linen trade of St. Gallen.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen grant Count Hugo von Königsegg und Rothenfels, Lord of Aulendorf and Staufen, Councillor of the Roman Imperial Majesty, at his request a postponement of the repayment of the loan and its outstanding interest at the Hospital, although the Hospital itself would be in need of the money due to general lack of funds and a purchase of property in the Rhine Valley.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich send to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen, in the enclosed attachment, a reply from Elector Karl Ludwig von der Pfalz concerning the transfer of 6000 Reichs thaler by the five Protestant cantons. Copies of the electoral reply have also been sent from Zürich to the other Protestant cantons.

Karl Ludwig von der Pfalz thanks the Protestant cantons of the Confederation for the loan of 6000 Reichsthaler, which he had requested and which has arrived with him. Karl Ludwig further thanks them for further testimonies of friendship as well as for the congratulations on his recently concluded marriage with Charlotte von Hessen-Kassel and assures the Protestant cantons in turn of his support and friendship. His messenger, who delivers these words of thanks, is to be believed in this regard.

The protected citizen of St. Gallen, Joachim Spengler, a glassworker in Konstanz, wishes to renounce his citizenship in St. Gallen. The Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen ask the Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz to send Spengler to St. Gallen for questioning and the renunciation of his citizenship.

Burgomaster and Council of Schaffhausen complain to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the delayed distribution of the inheritance of the St. Gallen citizen Bartholome Zollikofer to his relatives in Schaffhausen. Hieronymus Peyer complains on behalf of his mother about the claims of the widow Zollikofer, the St. Gallen citizen Margaretha Schobinger, which were raised anew after the end of the trial and are not prevented by the St. Gallen Council. As a result, trade goods of the family in Frankreich, Spanien, and Italien are being held up. The Schaffhausen authorities ask for support before the inheritance is distributed without an inventory.

Der administrator of the Hauptmannschaft, Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz report to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the citizen of St. Gallen and glassworker Joachim Spengler was admitted to the citizenship of Konstanz at his own and the request of several citizens of Konstanz. In order to obtain his birth certificate and his share of the inheritance in St. Gallen, Spengler granted power of attorney to his future brother-in-law, the citizen of Konstanz and Raiteschreiber Johann Pfeil, to collect both for him in St. Gallen. Therefore, Der administrator of the Hauptmannschaft, Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz ask for the acceptance and support of Johannes Pfeil in his tasks in St. Gallen.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen send two envoys, the Master Builder and Council member Cyrill Finsterling and the Council member Georg Zwicker, to Appenzell Ausser- and Innerrhoden, who will orally present the city's matter. It concerns a defamatory letter sent to the Diet by a bricklayer who is not further identified.

Maximilian, Pfalzgraf bei Rhein, Herzog in Ober- und Niederbayern und Erztruchsess und Kurfürst des Reichs, thanks the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for the friendly reception and the honors shown to his Privy Councillor Doctor Johann Adolph Krebs, who had stayed in St. Gallen for a time on business and, upon his return to München, had reported to Maximilian on his friendly reception. Maximilian assures the Burgomaster and Council of his goodwill.

The St. Gallen trading firm Hans Peter Konrad Fels and co-relatives request the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for a letter of recommendation in their name to the Ammann and Council of Uri, so that the Uri government will have the goods of the recently deceased Anna Thunbeysen from Baar, which they possess in Uri, seized, so that the debts still outstanding with the Fels brothers can be covered. The Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen have drawn up a corresponding petition to the Ammann and Council of Uri.

Schultheiss and Council of Winterthur report on the promise made before them by Pastor Hans Heinrich Krütli, citizen of Winterthur, to send 200 gulden to his daughter, who is engaged to the citizen of St. Gallen, Cornelius Kunz. This dowry is required by the town law of St. Gallen for the acceptance of women from outside, which is why Krütli, despite his previous refusal to give his daughter anything into the marriage during his lifetime, has agreed to the promise. Therefore, Burgomaster and Council of Winterthur ask Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to approve the marriage and to recognize Cornelius Kunz, as bearer of the letter, as the husband of the daughter.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request the count-fuggeric Council and Bailiff of Oberkirchberg and Burgomaster and Council of Ulm in two separate letters for support in the return of the property of the fatally accidented citizen of St. Gallen Johannes Locher. Locher was a messenger of Nürnberg and had drowned in the Danube. His horse and his belongings had been brought ashore at Oberkirchberg. His brother Jeremias Locher, citizen of St. Gallen and messenger of Lindau, had asked Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen in the name of the widow and children of Johannes Locher for the return of the horse, clothes, and property of the deceased, which is why Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen had two letters drawn up.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen ask Johann Rudolf Reding von Schwyz, Landvogt of Lichtensteig, to mediate in an inheritance division between Elisabeth Billwiler, wife of Jakob Locher, and her sister Dorothea Billwiler after the death of their mother Rosina Habmann. The sister Dorothea Billwiler is entitled to 200 gulden of marriage portion, which are to be taken from the estate, but without interest thereon. After deduction of the 200 gulden, the maternal property is to fall to the two sisters in equal halves.

A sender not named by name thanks personally and in the name of the Council of St. Gallen for the two wild calves presented as a gift to the Council, which had been brought to St. Gallen by the gamekeepers of Count Hugo von Montfort along with a letter. With the letter of thanks, a piece of St. Gallen linen is sent as a gift for the Count's wife, in the absence of anything better.

Burgomaster and Council of Ulm reply to a letter of thanks from Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen regarding the messenger of Nuremberg, Johannes Locher, who drowned at Gögglingen-Donaustetten. Burgomaster and Council of Ulm express their sympathy and inform that the body of Locher was found in the Danube following their ordered search and was honestly buried in the citizen's cemetery in Ulm. They wish to support Lott Specht of Ravensburg, who was authorized in this matter and sent to Ulm. Specht was already able to take the horse and bridle of the deceased into his hands at Oberkirchberg.

Burgomaster and Council of Überlingen send their Burgomaster, Doctor Johann Heinrich von Pflaumern, imperial councillor, to St. Gallen for certain matters. They ask the St. Gallen to grant an audience to their Burgomaster as the bearer of the letter of recommendation, to receive him, and to give credit to him and his statements.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request, in the name of their citizen Tobias Studer senior, Burgomaster and Council of Zürich to admit his son of the same name, Tobias Studer, to the Zucht- und Waisenhaus (House of Discipline and Orphans) at Oetenbach in Zürich. The institution admits disobedient children at the request of their parents and keeps them there to work. Tobias Studer junior suffers from madness and delusion and had started a quarrel in Mellingen over a crucifix. Therefore, it is feared in St. Gallen that he might trigger a conflict in the Abbey district, which is why the father would like to provide for his son in Zürich.

The administrator of the captaincy, the Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz request the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to support their citizen Joachim Spengler and his assistant Niklaus Schmidt, court clerk and citizen of Konstanz, during their stay in St. Gallen. Spengler, the bearer of the letter, wishes to marry the widow of the deceased citizen of Konstanz Michael Spengler and to redeem his birth certificates and his paternal property in St. Gallen for his newly acquired citizenship of Konstanz.

Diethelm Hegner zu Emmishofen again asks his brother-in-law Sebastian Schobinger, Doctor of Medicine and Burgomaster of St. Gallen, to use his influence to have a debt he owes to Junker Samuel Zollikofer forgiven. Hegner offers a debt in Marbach as compensation. If this is not approved, he asks that he be lent some money on his house. Hegner, as a citizen of St. Gallen, insists on clemency from the St. Gallen authorities or, if this cannot be obtained, from his brother-in-law. His honour depends on this matter.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request, in the name of all the bleachers of St. Gallen, the due interrogation and punishment of a linen thief who had stolen linen cloths on the bleach of the St. Gallen bleacher Kaspar Scheibener and who is now staying in Konstanz. The St. Gallen request an exemplary punishment of the perpetrator, as such crimes would severely harm not only St. Gallen but also the whole neighborhood. Furthermore, they request not only the interrogation of the perpetrator but also the examination of the St. Gallen citizen Marx Müller, who had harbored the linen thief in Wöschbach, and that of the bleacher Abraham von Konstanz. Both can provide information about the perpetrator. St. Gallen requests the sending of the written interrogations of all three. If Konstanz would prefer to hand the perpetrator over to the city of St. Gallen, Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen would cover the transport costs for this.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request the administrator of the captaincy, Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz, to hand over a linen thief apprehended in Konstanz. The request for handover, including the assumption of transport costs by St. Gallen, is justified by the location of the offense. Since the thefts had occurred in St. Gallen, the perpetrator should be interrogated and punished on the spot in St. Gallen and not in Konstanz. The St. Gallen authorities have already obtained permission from the Prince-Abbot's administration for the transport of the perpetrator through the territory.

The count's imperial marshal's Pappenheim officials of the lordship of Rothenstein ask the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for the second time for financial support for the construction of their evangelical church. The second funding request became necessary because the Catholic opponents, the monasteries of Augsburg and Kempten as well as Count Paul Fugger zu Kirchberg-Weißenhorn, prevented the evangelical church construction through various complaints and court days at the Imperial Diet in Nürnberg, thereby causing additional costs. Although it was not possible for the opponents to prevent the church construction, the financial means for the completion of the construction are now lacking. Therefore, they ask St. Gallen for renewed financial support.

Statthalter and Council of St. Gallen thank the Captaincy, Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz for the news of the capture and interrogation of Matthäus Mattler, who had stolen linen on the St. Gallen bleaching grounds. In the name of the bleaching masters of St. Gallen, Statthalter and Council of St. Gallen ask for the return of any St. Gallen linen that may turn up and for an appropriate punishment of the offender. Furthermore, Statthalter and Council of St. Gallen ask, in the name of the affected citizens of St. Gallen, the bleaching master Michael Schorno, Council member of Schwyz and Landvogt in Thurgau, for help in recovering the linen stolen by Matthäus Mattler. In the interrogation in Konstanz, he had admitted that he had sold the stolen St. Gallen linen cloths not only in the city of Konstanz but also in several places in Thurgau, in particular in an inn in Egelshofen.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request, in the name of their citizen Heinrich Giller the Younger, the assessors of the city court of Zürich for support in collecting the outstanding debts that Felix Burckhart, tanner and citizen of Zürich, owes to Giller. The debt disputes had already been heard twice before the city court of Zürich, whereby Burckhart was legally obligated to settle the debts. The payment deadlines set by the court have passed without any payment being received by Giller.

The administrator of the captaincy, the Burgomaster and Council of Konstanz inform the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the arrest and the amicable as well as the painful interrogation of the delinquent Matthäus Mattler from Ossingen. The people of Konstanz send as an enclosure excerpts from Mattler's confession that concern St. Gallen, and refer to the fact that the people of St. Gallen, after clarifications, can possibly influence in writing the scheduled hearing before the Malefizgericht.
This enclosure is the copy of the confession of Matthäus Mattler, who was arrested in Konstanz and had committed linen thefts on the St. Gallen bleaching greens.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen on a further support of the Reformed parish of Grünenbach for their newly erected church building. The Zürichers support the construction again with 150 gulden, as it is the only Protestant church in the otherwise Catholic and Lutheran surroundings. The Zürichers therefore ask the St. Galleners to also donate something. The money can be sent to the Zürich chancery, which collects and forwards all monetary donations of the Reformed cantons.

The Schultheiss and Council of Bern request the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to support their master Christoph Schüpfer from Erlach, whom they have equipped with this letter of recommendation and petition, in his matters locally in St. Gallen. Christoph Schüpfer represents his brother Daniel Schüpfer and his wife Anna Gonzenbach in an inheritance and usage dispute. It concerns 1500 gulden, which Anna Gonzenbach had left to her now deceased brother Heinrich Gonzenach for use. After his death, she demands this money back. The matter is prevented by the heirs because nothing is noted in the testament. With the remark that Schleissgüter do not have to be noted in the testament, the Schultheiss and Council of Bern request the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to support the petitioners.
