Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request Michael Schorno, Landvogt of the upper and lower Thurgau, in the name of their bleachers, to return without charge the linen stolen by Matthäus Mattler, which is partly located in the Thurgau, to them.

Landammann and Council of Appenzell Ausserrhoden request, with this letter of recommendation, the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to admit their citizen Konrad Bänziger, after completing his training as a cleric at the higher school in Zürich, to the examination in St. Gallen.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about a loan request by Herr Jacques Dupuys, former Consul of Montauban, for 200 doubloons, which he seeks from Evangelische towns and cantons. With the letter, the Zürichers forward two enclosures regarding the matter and ask for the opinion of the St. Gallen in this case. Identical letters were also sent to other Evangelische towns and cantons of the Confederation.
Loan request of Herr Jacques Dupuy to the Evangelical cantons of the Confederation Zürich, Bern, Basel and Schaffhausen.
Letter from Henri II. de Rohan with the parish priest Ambroise Faget to Jacques Dupuy concerning the religious disputes in La Rochelle.

Burgomaster and Council of Bludenz inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the first of the usual Bludenz markets in this year shall be moved from 2 to 3 October, as 2 October falls on a Sunday. Thereafter, the markets shall be held every 14 days until Christmas. Burgomaster and Council of Bludenz further defend themselves against rumors that a disease has broken out among the livestock offered at the market. Everyone may visit the market without concern and may demand a corresponding certificate.

Burgomaster and Council of Überlingen request Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for a postponement of the due annual interest payment for a loan. It is impossible for Überlingen, because of the imposed war burdens, to raise the funds.

Daniel Kessler der Jüngere reports to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen how he has fallen into a heavy burden of debt. He does not wish to simply make excuses, but stands by the serious errors he has made. He asks God, the authorities, and all whom he has offended for forgiveness. He wishes to replace the damage caused. However, he is concerned about the care of his children. Therefore, he has returned to the Unterpfalz and confessed his errors to the elector's church councilors and offered improvement. He was then appointed to the office of a Schuldiener. He would like to take his wife and children to him into the Schulhaus. However, he has no money. The children, however, still have some money, of which he wishes to use for the children's travel costs, provided the authorities permit this. Furthermore, he would have liked to ask for the maintenance of his citizenship, but because of his gross errors, he is not worthy of it until improvement and good behavior. However, his wife and children should not have to suffer under this, for which he asks the Burgomaster and Council. He asks for an answer.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen inform the Landvogt of Rorschach that the citizen of St. Gallen Elias Finsterling is accused of adultery. A woman named N. Rennhas is involved. The Landvogt is to order that the woman must appear before the Council in St. Gallen on the appointed date.

Burgomaster and Council of Überlingen inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that, following the conclusion of peace, the grain market in Überlingen is resumed. The merchants of St. Gallen had conducted active trade with Überlingen; they therefore ask that the old trust now return.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen answer Burgomaster and Council of Überlingen on their letter of 5. Oktober 1650, with which they had announced the resumption of the market in Überlingen and had asked their St. Gallen colleagues to instruct their merchants to visit the market again as before. Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen state that their merchants had complained about the high tolls in Überlingen. The merchants would participate in the market again as soon as the tolls were reduced again as in Radolfzell and in other places.

Burgomaster and Council of Lindau inform Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that the fair of Lindau, which was to take place on Friday 4 and Saturday 5 November, would not take place for various reasons. Lindau requests St. Gallen to inform those who had intended to visit the market, so that they would be spared unnecessary costs.

Bartholomäus Anhorn, pastor and inspector at Mosbach, reports to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about detrimental remarks and writings from citizens of St. Gallen, who would demand money from him. All his people in the office and inspection of Mosbach, including the ten parishes entrusted to him along with their church councils, would testify that the accusations are not justified. Anhorn requests the Burgomaster and Council to continue their goodwill towards him. To demonstrate his gratitude, he has had his farewell sermon printed, which he dedicates to the Burgomaster and Council. He will never erase St. Gallen from his memory.
It is a note by the St. Gallen clerk, who refers to the two letters from the year 1649 from Bartholomäus Anhorn, the pastor at Mosbach, which are already archived in the chancery.

Johann Jakob I. von Waldburg-Zeil reports to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that Johann Peter Escher, Colonel of the Lordship of Venedig, has lent him 800 silver crowns. To secure this, silver tableware was deposited, which is deposited with Hans Schlumpf in St. Gallen (see Obligation, Attachment 1). In the meantime, it has been possible for him, Count Johann Jakob, to acquire pledges located in the territory of Zürich, with which Escher is to be satisfied in place of the hypothecated silver tableware. Escher has agreed to this (see letter from Escher, Attachment 2). Count Johann Jakob subsequently entered into negotiations with Hans Ulrich Sulzer, Lord of the Court at Elgg. Escher’s wife learned of this and informed Peter Sulzer the Younger, whereupon the negotiations failed. The Count demanded that Escher prevent his wife from such interventions. He is now waiting for a reply from Escher. In the meantime, a letter from Johann Escher, Master of the Mint in Zürich, has been received. He conveys, in the name of the wife of Colonel Escher, that she had been required, in the absence of her husband, to repay recruitment funds taken on credit. Therefore, she must resort to the pledge (silver tableware), and the Count should send a lawyer to St. Gallen. The Count does not agree with this, especially since the recruitment funds taken on credit do not concern him and the wife of the Colonel is herself to blame for the delay. Moreover, the obligation issued by the Count does not provide for such realization of the pledge. The Count requests the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen that, in the event that a representative of Escher comes to St. Gallen and wishes to attack the pledge, they do not permit this, but ask the representative for patience until the reply of Colonel Escher arrives or the Count has other means available again, of which the wife of the Colonel must not be informed too early. However, if she should nevertheless be able to attack the pledge, he, the Count, will claim costs and damages.

Johann Jakob I. von Waldburg-Zeil certifies that Johann Peter Escher, Colonel of the Lordship of Venedig and Master of Ordnance of Zürich, has lent him 800 silver crowns. The loan is to be repaid in one year after Martini (11 November) with interest. As security, the Count pledges his silver tableware, which is located with Hans Schlumpf in St. Gallen. Furthermore, a fief belonging to the County, worth 500 Rhenish gulden, is assigned to the lender as security.

Johann Peter Escher, Obrist of the Herrschaft Venedig, confirms to Johann Jakob I. von Waldburg-Zeil that he accepts the fief offered by the Count as a pledge and releases the pledge (silverware) located in St. Gallen. The obligation issued by the Count mentions only 800 ducats (silver crowns), but he has additionally sent the Count twice 50 ducats. The Count may send the obligation to Zürich to his (Escher's) wife. If the obligation is found to be in order by her, he will accept the obligation. Otherwise, he knows nothing of the aforementioned ill repute concerning this transaction, and he distances himself from it.

Maximilian, hereditary marshal and landgrave of Stühlingen, requests the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to grant an audience to his castle captain Antonius Gerber. He will then present the matter orally in his name. Maximilian asks the Burgomaster and Council to give Gerber good faith.

The Stadtvogt and Council of Maienfeld answer the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen regarding their letter of 14 January 1650 (Missive No. 3994) in favor of St. Gallen creditors of the Glarner Rudolf Elmer. Now, however, their citizen and at the same time subject of Glarus, Hans Heinrich Stäger, has placed an arrest on Elmer's assets located in Maienfeld. According to treaties and alliances, however, the Stadtvogt and Council of Maienfeld cannot lift the arrest without the knowledge and will of the authority of Glarus. The Stadtvogt and Council would, however, request Glarus to order that the arrest be lifted.

Pappenheimische officials of the lordship of Rothenstein thank the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen for their assistance with the church construction. St. Gallen had supported the effort twice with a so-called building tax of 250 florins each, so that the Reformed church in Grönenbach, which had been burned down in the Thirty Years' War, could be rebuilt.

Burgomaster and Council of Zürich complain to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about the sinful way of life of the people, which has aroused the holy wrath of God. This wrath has manifested itself since the beginning of the century in earthquakes and other signs. In order that the enraged God may be appeased again and refrain from further punishments, Burgomaster and Council of Zürich have instructed the city and countryside not to begin the new year of the second half of the century with excessive eating and drinking, but with fasting, praying, and doing penance. Burgomaster and Council wished to report this not only to St. Gallen, but also to the other evangelical cantons.

Burgomaster and Council of Ravensburg report to Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen about their citizen, Johannes Schlappritzi, who owes 450 florins to his brother-in-law, Johannes Högger, citizen and chandler of St. Gallen. Schlaprizi has issued a debt acknowledgment to Högger. After payments became due in the autumn, Högger demanded them from Schlappritzi, who is not in a position to make them, especially as he himself has outstanding claims against third parties. As long as these claims are not settled in his favor, he cannot pay Högger. Therefore, he has asked Burgomaster and Council of Ravensburg for support in his favor with Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen. Schlaprizi asks Högger for patience. Burgomaster and Council of Ravensburg join the request, especially as Schlaprizi has not settled the claim of Högger intentionally, willfully, or negligently.

Hans Bernhard Ströbel, citizen and innkeeper at the Drei Kronen in Nürnberg, requests the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to compel their citizen Georg Basthard, bookbinder in St. Gallen, to pay him a long-overdue and acknowledged debt of 38 1/2 florins, together with interest and costs amounting to approximately 23 florins. The debtor still has sufficient means at his disposal; he has simply, in the manner of bad payers, willfully taken to the lazy side. Should he continue to refuse, the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen are asked to seize the property of Basthard.

Johann Michael Wagner, Amtmann of the Lordship of Langenargen, reports to the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen on behalf of Count Hugo zu Montfort, Lord of Bregenz, Tettnang and Langenargen, that the citizen of St. Gallen Kaspar Haltmeyer, called Güggi, had started a conflict with Hans Muffler, citizen and butcher of Langenargen, in the lower and high judicial jurisdiction of the Lordship of Langenargen. Wagner requests the Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen to summon Güggi, so that he, since the conflict had broken out in Langenargen, should give an account and answer before the Count there.

Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen address Ammann and Court of Thal on behalf of their citizen Johannes Berung. It concerns a claim of 30 florins plus interest against Christof Kuon. Berung was awarded the amount by the court as child support. He has received nothing yet. Burgomaster and Council of St. Gallen request Ammann and Court of Thal to support the claim against Berungs.

The preachers of the County of Hanau remind the preaching office of St. Gallen of their request for support. They say that a year ago they had written to four evangelical churches of the Confederation. Bern and Zürich had helped. However, no answer had been received from St. Gallen, which is why they ask whether the letter had arrived. After further warlike actions had again caused great distress, they urgently request help once more.
